FLicc user guide

Multi-gear length-interval catch-curve analysis in FLR

Henning Winker (FAO-NFI)

21 October 2026

1 FLicc: a framework for length-interval catch curves

FLicc fits length-interval catch curves (ICC): equilibrium models that explain the length composition of the catch by growth, natural mortality, fishing mortality and selectivity, integrated over length intervals (bins). It brings the two main lines of length-based per-recruit assessment into one framework, built on FLR (Kell et al. 2007) and fitted with TMB (Kristensen et al. 2016):

  • fishblicc (Medley 2025), whose formulation FLicc follows most closely: steady-state length-interval survival with individual Linf gamma-distributed around the von Bertalanffy mean, constant mortality within each length interval, several gears with their own selectivity (logistic, normal and double-sided normal), and a negative-binomial likelihood. FLicc’s pop_model = "gamma" with obs_model = "nb" reproduces this setup (Reproducing fishblicc); FLicc fits it by maximum likelihood in TMB instead of Bayesian estimation in Stan.
  • LBSPR (Hordyk et al. 2015, 2016), whose growth-type-group (GTG) formulation is FLicc’s default population model (pop_model = "gtg"): Linf varies between growth-type groups, each with its own survival through the length classes, and status is expressed as the spawning potential ratio.
  • LBB (Froese et al. 2018), the length-based Bayesian biomass estimator, which is nested in the GTG model: one growth type, one gear, each year fitted separately, with priors on Linf and M/K. lbb_flicc() sets FLicc up as LBB, and LBB’s status measure B/B0 (exploited biomass relative to unfished) is available for any FLicc fit as the exploitable potential ratio (EPR; Reproducing LBB).

Each of these tools is a configuration of FLicc:

Tool FLicc configuration
LBSPR pop_model = "gtg" (ngtg = 13, maxsd = 2, CVL 0.1), obs_model = "mn", Linf, M/k and CVL fixed, by_year = TRUE
LBB lbb_flicc(): pop_model = "gtg" with ngtg = 1, obs_model = "dm" (fixed precision; ess = 20000 matches LBB’s Dirichlet), priors on Linf and M/k, by_year = TRUE, pile = 0 or 1
fishblicc pop_model = "gamma", obs_model = "nb", several gears, catch shares in numbers
FLicc default pop_model = "gtg", obs_model = "dm" with the precision estimated (dm_theta = "saturating"), all years jointly with a random walk on F

Each configuration is reproduced on the tool’s own example data, and compared with FLicc’s default, in section Reproducing LBSPR, LBB and fishblicc.

On this common basis FLicc adds what a routine assessment and management procedure needs: several years fitted jointly with shared selectivity and a random walk on F, alternative observation models (multinomial, Dirichlet-multinomial with estimated precision, negative binomial), treatment of the tail of the composition, reference points with steepness, length-based indicators, residual diagnostics, and use as the estimation model of an MSE in FLR.

The names of the models and options in FLicc credit these sources: fishblicc for the length-interval catch-curve formulation, multi-gear selectivity and the gamma growth model; LBSPR for the GTG model and the SPR-based use of length data in data-limited fisheries; LBB for the single-growth-type special case, its priors and the B/B0 status measure.

1.1 About this guide

The guide is in three parts. Part I goes through an assessment from the data to stock status: length-frequency data (including missing data), life history, selectivity, fitting and diagnostics, reference points and status, and length-based indicators, with explicit checks at each step (what to look at, what is a red flag, what to do about it). Part II documents the technical options for users who need them: effective sample size and observation models, fishing mortality over time, growth variability and life-history priors, the tail of the composition, the model equations and a comparison of models, and the reproduction of LBSPR, LBB and fishblicc. Part III covers use in management-strategy evaluation and summarises the checks and recommendations. The examples use the built-in splendid alfonsino data. Recommendations marked simulation come from tests with an alfonsino-like operating model (fixed-CV length-at-age, annual recruitment, Beverton-Holt h = 0.75, two gears, two-stage length sampling). Monte-Carlo ensembles over life-history uncertainty (mc_flicc()) will be documented separately.

2 Installation

FLicc depends on FLCore, ggplotFL and TMB. On Windows, compiling the TMB model requires Rtools (https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/).

install.packages("TMB", type = "source")
install.packages(c("FLCore", "ggplotFL"),
                 repos = c("https://flr.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
remotes::install_github("henning-winker/FLicc")                    # release
remotes::install_github("henning-winker/FLicc", ref = "dev-merge")  # development
library(FLicc)
packageVersion("FLicc")
#> [1] '1.0.11'

3 Quick start: your first fit

This section goes from a table of length measurements to a first fitted model and its main plots, using the default settings. The later sections explain each step, the checks to make and the options.

3.1 Step 1: length data as a table

FLicc needs length-frequency counts by length bin, year and gear (fleet). The simplest starting point is a long table with one row per bin, year and gear, and the columns len (lower bound of the length bin), year, data (number of fish measured) and qname (gear name). The alfonsino example data in this format:

library(FLicc)
data("alfonsino")
lfd_df <- as.data.frame(lfd_alfonsino)[, c("len", "year", "data", "qname")]
head(lfd_df)
#>   len year data qname
#> 1   5 2013    0 Trawl
#> 2   6 2013    0 Trawl
#> 3   7 2013    0 Trawl
#> 4   8 2013    0 Trawl
#> 5   9 2013    0 Trawl
#> 6  10 2013    0 Trawl
unique(lfd_df$qname)       # gears
#> [1] Trawl   Gillnet
#> Levels: Trawl Gillnet
range(lfd_df$len)          # length range (cm)
#> [1]  5 67
range(lfd_df$year)         # years
#> [1] 2013 2024

For your own data, read the file and name the columns accordingly, for example:

lfd_df <- read.csv("my_length_data.csv")              # columns: length, year, count, fleet
names(lfd_df) <- c("len", "year", "data", "qname")

3.2 Step 2: convert to FLQuants

lfd_long_to_wide() turns the long table into a wide one (one column per year, missing combinations filled with zeros), and FLQuantLen() turns that into an FLQuants object with one FLQuant per gear. midL = FALSE says that len is the lower bound of each bin; use midL = TRUE if your lengths are bin mid-points. Lengths in mm can be converted with unit = "mm".

lfd <- FLQuantLen(lfd_long_to_wide(lfd_df), unit = "cm", midL = FALSE)
names(lfd)
#> [1] "Trawl"   "Gillnet"

3.3 Step 3: look at the data

plot_lfd(lfd)

Each panel is a year, each colour a gear. Check that the compositions look plausible: one main mode per gear, no sudden shifts between years, no fish far beyond the expected maximum length.

3.4 Step 4: life history

Growth, natural mortality, maturity and the length-weight relationship are given as an FLPar:

Parameter Meaning
linf, k von Bertalanffy asymptotic length and growth rate
M natural mortality (per year)
L50 length at 50% maturity
a, b weight-length relationship W=aLbW = aL^b (here weight in kg for length in cm) 
lhpar <- FLPar(linf = 55.7, k = 0.08, M = 0.162, L50 = 31.1859,
               a = 0.004721956 / 1000, b = 3.146168)

3.5 Step 5: the stock object and natural mortality

stocklen() combines the length data and the life history into an FLStockLen object with weight, maturity and natural mortality at length. m_model sets how natural mortality changes with length:

m_model M at length
"constant" the same M at all lengths (default choice)
"inverse" MLref/LM\,L_{ref}/L, higher for small fish; needs reflen
"Lorenzen" allometric, decreasing with weight
"Gislason" empirical, depending on length and Linf 
stklen <- stocklen(lfd, lhpar, m_model = "constant")
plot_m(stklen)

plot_mat(stklen)

Start with "constant" unless there is a biological reason for a length-dependent M.

3.6 Step 6: fit the model

Two inputs are always needed besides the data and the stock object, both with one entry per gear in the order of names(lfd) (here Trawl, Gillnet):

  • sel_fun: the shape of each gear’s selectivity. "logistic" for gears that keep catching the largest fish (asymptotic, e.g. most trawls and longlines); "dsnormal" (double-sided normal) for gears that catch mostly intermediate sizes and fewer large fish (dome-shaped, e.g. gillnets with one mesh size, or fleets fishing where large fish are scarce). Here the trawl catches small fish and few large ones, the gillnet the larger fish.
  • catch_by_gear: the share of the total catch taken by each gear, e.g. c(0.95, 0.05) for 95% and 5%. It tells the model how to split F between the gears; FLicc matches it to the predicted catch in weight, so the shares of the landings in tonnes can be used directly.
fit1 <- fiticc(lfd, stklen,
               sel_fun = c("dsnormal", "logistic"),
               catch_by_gear = c(0.95, 0.05))

All other settings are at their defaults: growth and M fixed at the input values, a Dirichlet-multinomial likelihood on the counts as they are, with its precision estimated from the data (so the counts need no rescaling), and a random walk on F over the years.

3.7 Step 7: check and plot the results

First check that the fit converged: all lines should show passed = TRUE.

flicc_convergence(fit1)
#>                              check              value passed
#> 2           Gradient is acceptable          5.704e-05   TRUE
#> 3     Hessian is positive definite               TRUE   TRUE
#> 4        Standard errors available 31 / 31 parameters   TRUE
#> 5 Hessian eigenvalues are positive              14.22   TRUE
#> 6   Newton decrement is negligible           2.38e-13   TRUE
#> 7                          Overall                 ok   TRUE
#>                                                                                        interpretation
#> 2                                                             The fit is close to a stationary point.
#> 3                                                                The model curvature is well behaved.
#> 4                                                  Uncertainty could be estimated for all parameters.
#> 5                                             No flat or negative curvature directions were detected.
#> 6 Expected further gain in log-likelihood (0.5 g'H^-1 g) is below 0.001; NA without Newton polishing.
#> 7              ok: converged; warning: usable, but check the gradient or decrement; fail: do not use.

The fitted (lines) against the observed (bars) length compositions

plot_len(fit1)

also shown by gear

plot_len(fit1, by_gear = TRUE,year=2020:2024)

The estimated selectivity of each gear:

plot_sel(fit1)

The spawning potential ratio (SPR) by year with its 95% interval, and the value in the last year. SPR is the spawning output per recruit at the estimated F relative to the unfished state; 40% is a common target.

plot_spr(fit1, ci = TRUE)

sprcur_flicc(fit1)
#> [1] 0.1660614

That is a first assessment. Before using it, work through the checks of the following sections. The default likelihood estimates how much weight the length data can carry (section Effective sample size and observation models); it works best with the raw counts, as here, or an effective sample size of at least 500 per gear and year. The reference fit used in the rest of this guide (next section) is this default configuration.

4 Workflow and defaults

  1. Data: length frequencies by gear as FLQuants (Quick start); check sample sizes, gaps and the tail.
  2. Life history: FLPar and stocklen(); check Linf against the largest fish.
  3. Selectivity: choose the shape per gear; dome sensitivity.
  4. Fit: fiticc(); check convergence, residuals, selectivity and retrospective consistency.
  5. Status: SPR, Fspr, steepness-corrected biomass, length-based indicators.
  6. Uncertainty: sensitivity runs (selectivity dome, CVL, Linf, tail cut), fits_summary() and ensemble_flicc().
  7. Management: flicc.sa() and harvest control rules in an MSE.

A plain fiticc() call uses the GTG population model, a Dirichlet-multinomial likelihood with the precision estimated from the data, fixed growth (Linf, CVL) and natural mortality, and a random walk on log F with its standard deviation fixed at sigmaF = 0.3. Give it the raw counts or an effective sample size of at least 500 per gear and year. Every other option is a deliberate change.

4.1 The reference fit

The rest of the guide uses one reference fit of the alfonsino data: the raw counts, a double-sided normal (dome) selectivity for the trawl and a logistic one for the gillnet, catch shares of 95% and 5% by weight, CVL = 0.1, and the default Dirichlet-multinomial likelihood with the precision estimated from the data (dm_theta = "saturating", section Effective sample size and observation models; given explicitly below for clarity).

sel_fun <- c("dsnormal", "logistic")
cbg <- c(0.95, 0.05)
fit <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
              settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"))
sprcur_flicc(fit)
#> [1] 0.1660614

Part I: Assessment basics

5 Length-frequency data

5.1 Structure

data("alfonsino")
lfd <- FLQuantLen(lfd_long_to_wide(as.data.frame(lfd_alfonsino)), unit = "cm", midL = FALSE)
names(lfd)
#> [1] "Trawl"   "Gillnet"
range(as.numeric(dimnames(lfd[[1]])$len)); range(as.numeric(dimnames(lfd[[1]])$year))
#> [1]  5 67
#> [1] 2013 2024

FLQuantLen() takes a wide table (lfd_long_to_wide() converts a long one) with columns for length, year, gear and counts; midL = FALSE means lengths are lower bin boundaries. Bins must be equally spaced and identical across gears and years (complete_lfd_bins() fills gaps with zeros).

5.2 Check 1: sample size by year and gear

plot_lfdn(lfd)

Why The information in a composition depends on how many independent samples (trips, hauls, landings) it comes from, not only on the number of fish.
Look for Gear-years with very few fish or few occupied bins (labels), years where one gear is missing, strong changes in the gear mix between years.
Red flags Gear-years with < 50 fish or < 10 occupied bins; a gear present only in some years; combined sample size dominated by one gear in some years and another in others.
Action Set effective sample sizes per gear (section Effective sample size and observation models); consider dropping or pooling very poor gear-years; check that catch_by_gear reflects the catch, not the sampling, split.

5.3 Check 2: consistency of the compositions

plot_lfd(lfd, type = "relmax")

Look for Stable shapes and modes between adjacent years; similar left limbs within a gear (selectivity is assumed constant over time).
Red flags Abrupt shifts in the mode or left limb (change of gear, mesh, market sorting or sampling programme); bimodal compositions from mixing gears or areas; truncation at the right (size limits, sorting).
Action Split gears or periods with different selectivity; restrict years; investigate sampling before modelling around it.

5.4 Check 3: the largest fish

linf_in <- 55.7
sapply(lfd, function(x) {
  L <- as.numeric(dimnames(x)$len); n <- apply(x@.Data, 1, sum)
  c(max_length = max(L[n > 0]), pct_ge_0.9Linf = round(100 * sum(n[L >= 0.9 * linf_in]) / sum(n), 1),
    pct_ge_Linf = round(100 * sum(n[L >= linf_in]) / sum(n), 2))
})
#>                Trawl Gillnet
#> max_length        53   57.00
#> pct_ge_0.9Linf     0    0.40
#> pct_ge_Linf        0    0.06
Why The tail is the part of the composition most sensitive to Linf, CVL, dome-shaped selectivity and the GTG discretisation.
Red flags More than about 1% of fish at or above the input Linf; a long thin tail far beyond Linf (misidentified species, measurement errors, other stocks).
Action Re-examine Linf; use a tail cut (section Tail of the length composition) or rob_eps; fiticc() warns about fish beyond the largest growth group (tail_warning, default TRUE).

5.5 Check 4: empirical catch curves

A log-linear catch curve on the length-converted ages gives a quick, model-free view of total mortality by year and of its trend:

lhpar <- FLPar(linf = 55.7, k = 0.08, M = 0.162, L50 = 31.1859,
               a = 0.004721956 / 1000, b = 3.146168)
plot_zlcc(lfd$Trawl, lhpar)

plot_zlcc(lfd$Gillnet, lhpar)

Look for Roughly linear descending limbs; a stable or smoothly changing slope (Z).
Red flags Strongly curved descending limbs (dome-shaped selectivity, recruitment pulses), slopes jumping between years (sampling noise or changing selectivity).
Action Consider dsnormal selectivity or a tail cut; expect noisy annual F and keep the random walk.

5.6 Missing data

FLicc handles missing gear-years directly: a gear-year without samples (all zero counts) contributes nothing to the composition likelihood, and its F is informed by the random walk on F from neighbouring years (section Fishing mortality over time) and by the catch-share constraint. The example removes the gillnet samples of 2016 and 2017 and the trawl samples of 2020 and refits the reference model.

lfd_miss <- lfd
lfd_miss[["Gillnet"]][, c("2016", "2017","2022")] <- 0
lfd_miss[["Trawl"]][, c("2020","2022")] <- 0
fit_miss <- fiticc(lfd_miss, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                   settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"))
flicc_convergence(fit_miss)
#>                              check              value passed
#> 2           Gradient is acceptable          1.799e-05   TRUE
#> 3     Hessian is positive definite               TRUE   TRUE
#> 4        Standard errors available 31 / 31 parameters   TRUE
#> 5 Hessian eigenvalues are positive              10.32   TRUE
#> 6   Newton decrement is negligible           1.29e-13   TRUE
#> 7                          Overall                 ok   TRUE
#>                                                                                        interpretation
#> 2                                                             The fit is close to a stationary point.
#> 3                                                                The model curvature is well behaved.
#> 4                                                  Uncertainty could be estimated for all parameters.
#> 5                                             No flat or negative curvature directions were detected.
#> 6 Expected further gain in log-likelihood (0.5 g'H^-1 g) is below 0.001; NA without Newton polishing.
#> 7              ok: converged; warning: usable, but check the gradient or decrement; fail: do not use.
plot_lfdn(lfd_miss)

plot_spr(list(complete = fit, gaps = fit_miss), ci = TRUE)

Guidelines:

Situation Handling
a gear missing in some years keep the zeros; the random walk bridges them (intervals widen)
all gears missing in a year leave the year in (F interpolated) or restrict years
long gaps or a gear only at the start or end consider fitting the gear’s period separately; selectivity is assumed constant
no random walk (prior_sigmaF = FALSE) avoid with gaps: F of a gear-year without data is not identified
by_year = TRUE fits only years with data; selectivity per year
catch by gear missing use the average split; it only enters through the catch-share constraint

6 Life history and the stock object

stklen
#> An object of class "FLStockLen"
#> 
#> Name: FLicc stocklen 
#> Description:  
#> Quant: len 
#> Dims:  len   year    unit    season  area    iter
#>  63  12  1   1   1   1   
#> 
#> Range:  min  max minyear maxyear minfbar maxfbar 
#>  5   67  2013    2024    5   67

stocklen(lfd, lhpar, m_model) builds the length-based stock object: weight W(L)=aLbW(L) = aL^b, maturity as a logistic ogive with L50 and L95 (default L95 = L50 + 0.2 Linf), and natural mortality at length:

m_model M(L)M(L)
"constant" MM
"inverse" MLref/LM\, L_{ref}/L
"Lorenzen" Lorenzen weight-based, scaled to MM at reflen
"Gislason" Gislason et al. (2010) from LL, L∞L_\infty, kk

The length model uses M/kM/k (and Z/kZ/k): what matters is the ratio, so k and M uncertainty should be considered jointly (as in mc_flicc()).

6.1 Check 5: life-history inputs

Look for Linf close to the largest regularly observed lengths (Check 3); M/k near the life-history invariant range (often 1-2); L50 below the modal length of the main gear.
Red flags Linf well below the largest fish (many fish beyond Linf) or far above it; Linf from another region or sex; M/k outside 0.5-3 without justification.
Action Linf is the dominant sensitivity (simulation: a 10% error shifts SPR by +75% / -30%); run Linf sensitivities and include Linf in the ensemble.

7 Selectivity

7.1 Functions and parameterisation

Selectivity is specified per gear in sel_fun and estimated on a scale relative to Linf (log parameters θ\theta), so starting values and priors are scale-free. With the estimated Linf:

Logistic ("logistic"): S(L)=[1+exp(−ln19L−L50L95−L50)]−1,L50=eθ1L∞,L95−L50=eθ2L∞. S(L) = \left[1 + \exp\left(-\ln 19\,\frac{L - L_{50}}{L_{95} - L_{50}}\right)\right]^{-1}, \quad L_{50} = e^{\theta_1} L_\infty,\; L_{95} - L_{50} = e^{\theta_2} L_\infty .

Double-sided normal ("dsnormal", dome): S(L)=exp[−(L−Lmode)22σ2],σ={σLL<LmodeσRL≥Lmode,Lmode=eθ1L∞,σL=eθ2L∞,σR=eθ3L∞. S(L) = \exp\left[-\frac{(L - L_{mode})^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],\quad \sigma = \begin{cases}\sigma_L & L < L_{mode}\\ \sigma_R & L \ge L_{mode}\end{cases}, \quad L_{mode} = e^{\theta_1}L_\infty,\; \sigma_L = e^{\theta_2}L_\infty,\; \sigma_R = e^{\theta_3}L_\infty .

Normal ("normal"): as above with σL=σR\sigma_L = \sigma_R.

Two size modes ("binormal", "bidsnormal"): for gears whose catch has two size groups, e.g. juveniles and adults in different seasons, or a gillnet fleet with two mesh groups. The selectivity is the sum of two curves, scaled to a maximum of 1: S(L)=s(L)maxLs(L),s(L)=exp[−(L−L1)22σ12]+hexp[−(L−L2)22σ22], S(L) = \frac{s(L)}{\max_L s(L)},\quad s(L) = \exp\left[-\frac{(L - L_{1})^2}{2\sigma_1^2}\right] + h\,\exp\left[-\frac{(L - L_{2})^2}{2\sigma_2^2}\right], with the first mode L1L_1 (mode1, SD sd1), the second mode L2>L1L_2 > L_1 (mode2) and hh (h), the height of the second curve relative to the first. "binormal" uses one SD for the second curve (sd2); "bidsnormal" makes it double-sided (lsd2 to the left, rsd2 to the right of L2L_2), so the right limb of the large-fish mode can be domed or, with rsd2 = 1000 fixed, flat. These functions have five and six parameters and need enough data in both modes: with few samples the second curve can degenerate (e.g. a vertical step).

Starting values: the mode (or L50) at the gear’s observed modal length, spreads of 0.1 Linf. Selectivity is evaluated at bin mid-points and is constant over time.

plot_sel(fit)

selpars_flicc(fit)
#> An object of class "FLPars"
#> [[1]]
#> An object of class "FLPar"
#> params
#>  mode   lsd   rsd 
#> 23.83  3.33 19.44 
#> units:  cm 
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> An object of class "FLPar"
#> params
#> SL50 SL95 
#> 30.4 36.4 
#> units:  cm 
#> 
#> Slot "names":
#> [1] "Trawl"   "Gillnet"
#> 
#> Slot "desc":
#> character(0)
#> 
#> Slot "lock":
#> [1] FALSE

7.2 Fixing selectivity parameters

sel_fixed fixes parameters on the length scale by gear, e.g. from mesh experiments:

fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
       settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"),
       sel_fixed = list(Gillnet = list(SL50 = 30, SL95 = 34)))   # logistic
# dsnormal: list(mode = 24, lsd = 3, rsd = 1000)  (rsd = 1000: flat right limb)
# normal:   list(mode = 24, sd = 4)
# binormal:   list(mode1 = 15, sd1 = 2, mode2 = 30, sd2 = 5, h = 0.5)
# bidsnormal: list(mode1 = 15, sd1 = 2, mode2 = 30, lsd2 = 4, rsd2 = 1000, h = 0.5)

7.3 Exploring selectivity shapes

plot_selfun() draws a selectivity function for a range of parameter values, over the observed composition of a gear and with reference lengths. It helps to choose values for sel_fixed and the dome scenarios below:

gn <- lfd[["Gillnet"]]
Lmid_g <- as.numeric(dimnames(gn)$len) + 0.5
Lmean_g <- round(sum(Lmid_g * apply(gn, 1, sum)) / sum(gn), 1)
Lmean_g
#> [1] 33.3

ref_L <- c(L50mat = 31.2, Lmean = Lmean_g, Linf = 55.7)
plot_selfun("dsnormal", list(mode = 34, lsd = 4, rsd = c(1000, round(c(0.85, 0.7, 0.55, 0.4) * 55.7, 1))),
            lfd = gn, ref = ref_L)

plot_selfun("logistic", list(SL50 = c(28, 31, 34), SL95 = 37), lfd = gn, ref = ref_L[c(1,3)])

A double-sided normal with a very large right-hand SD (rsd = 1000) has a flat right limb, i.e. no dome; smaller values give increasing doming. The values shown, c(1000, 0.85, 0.7, 0.55, 0.4) x Linf, are the default levels of the dome sensitivity below, from no dome to a moderate one. sel_curve_flicc() returns the values of a curve.

The two-mode functions are explored the same way. A composition with two size modes arises, for example, when the gears are pooled into one fleet. combine_lfd() pools the gears, each raised by its catch share (for this example by weight, cbg = 70% trawl, 30% gillnet), and rescales the result to an effective sample size:

yr_last  <- tail(as.numeric(dimnames(lfd[[1]])$year), 1)
lfd_fleet <- combine_lfd(window(lfd, start = yr_last), catch_by_gear = c(0.7,0.3) ,
                         lhpar = lhpar, ess.n = 500)
plot_lfd(window(lfd, start = yr_last))

plot_lfd(lfd_fleet)

The pooled fleet has a small-fish mode (from the trawl) at about 18 cm and a large-fish mode (mainly from the gillnet) at about 31 cm. Over it, "binormal" with two widths of the second curve, and "bidsnormal" with the second mode flat (rsd2 = 1000, asymptotic) or domed on the right:

plot_selfun("binormal", list(mode1 = 22, sd1 = 3.3, mode2 = 31, sd2 = c(3, 8), h = 0.8),
            lfd = lfd_fleet, ref = ref_L)

plot_selfun("bidsnormal", list(mode1 = 22, sd1 = 3.3, mode2 = 31, lsd2 = 3,
                               rsd2 = c(1000, 10, 4), h = 0.7),
            lfd = lfd_fleet, ref = ref_L)

These curves are fitted to the pooled fleet in section Sensitivity runs and ensembles: a single year.

7.4 Gear selectivity, availability and population selectivity

The selectivity Sg(L)S_g(L) that FLicc estimates for a gear is not the selectivity of the gear itself (its contact or mesh selectivity) but the population selectivity: the relative fishing mortality at length for the stock as a whole, which combines the gear’s contact selectivity with the availability of fish of each size to where the fleet fishes. Sampson and Scott (2011) showed with a spatial model of linked subpopulations that population selectivity becomes dome-shaped even when every subpopulation is fished with the same asymptotic gear, unless fishing mortality is uniform across them: older fish accumulate in less-fished areas, a “cryptic biomass” that escapes capture. The shape depends on the gear, the level and spatial distribution of fishing effort, and the movement of fish between areas.

Consequences for FLicc:

  • A logistic gear does not imply logistic population selectivity. The question is whether the fleet’s fishing mortality reaches the large fish in proportion, not only what the mesh or hook does.
  • Slight doming is a plausible state of nature, particularly where large fish move deeper, offshore or into areas that are fished less. This is the rationale for running the dome sensitivity routinely (next section) and, where the doming level is uncertain, for integrating it with ensemble_flicc().
  • The dome is an assumption about fish that are not seen. A fitted dome tells the model that large fish are present but not caught, so they continue to grow and spawn, and SPR increases. That is right if they are in a refuge, and optimistic if they are missing because they died (higher F or natural mortality of large fish). Length data alone cannot separate the two, and a better likelihood for a stronger dome is not evidence that the cryptic biomass exists; the doming level should be informed by knowledge of the fishery and the stock’s distribution.
  • Data by area can be used as separate gears (“areas as fleets”): each area then has its own selectivity, which removes the part of the dome that comes from mixing areas with different size compositions.
  • The tail cut conditions on the fish below the cut and so reduces the dependence on the assumed dome, which acts on the largest fish.
  • Because population selectivity depends on where and how hard the fleet fishes, it can change when the effort distribution changes substantially. With a stable fishery a constant selectivity is a reasonable assumption; a change of sign of the residuals between periods (section Residual diagnostics) is the signal to check.
Situation Population selectivity In FLicc
Fleet covers the stock’s range evenly, or fish mix well close to gear selectivity logistic base; dome sensitivity as a check
Fishing concentrated where small and mid-sized fish are; large fish less available dome plausible dome sensitivity; ensemble over mild to moderate domes or tail cut
Length data available by area dome partly from the mix of areas areas as separate gears
Substantial change in where or how the fleet fishes may change check residuals by period; by_year

Reference: Sampson, D.B. and Scott, R.D. (2011). A spatial model for fishery age-selection at the population level. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences. doi:10.1139/f2011-044.

7.5 Dome sensitivity: a recommended standard run

Slight doming (large fish less selected or less available) is hard to detect from length data, and an unmodelled dome is read as higher F. A sensitivity over fixed dome shapes is therefore recommended for every gear assumed logistic. dome_sens_flicc() refits the model with that gear as a double-sided normal whose right-hand SD is fixed at a sequence of values (default c(1000, 0.85, 0.7, 0.55, 0.4) x Linf, from a flat right limb to a moderate dome in even steps; stronger domes can be given with rsd); the mode and left-hand SD are estimated, all other settings and data as in the base fit.

ds <- dome_sens_flicc(fit, gear = "Gillnet")
ds$table
#>   scenario    rsd conv    logLik      AIC SPR_last   Fspr Fap_last  dAIC
#> 1     base     NA    0 -36979.56 74021.12    0.166 0.0900   0.1950  0.00
#> 2  rsd1000 1000.0    0 -36986.52 74035.05    0.165 0.0895   0.1950 13.93
#> 3  rsd47.3   47.3    0 -36985.87 74033.75    0.169 0.0906   0.1935 12.63
#> 4    rsd39   39.0    0 -36985.55 74033.10    0.171 0.0911   0.1927 11.98
#> 5  rsd30.6   30.6    0 -36984.89 74031.77    0.176 0.0923   0.1910 10.65
#> 6  rsd22.3   22.3    0 -36983.16 74028.33    0.189 0.0952   0.1864  7.21
plot_dome_sens(ds)

plot_dome_sens(ds, "spr", ci = TRUE)

The run with rsd = 1000 reproduces the logistic base fit (SPR 0.165 vs 0.166), which is the check that the scenarios are comparable. For the gillnet the dome levels fit about equally well (dAIC 13.93, 12.63, 11.98, 10.65, 7.21 from no to moderate doming). The data therefore cannot tell whether large fish are fully selected or somewhat less so, and over that range the last-year SPR goes from 0.165 to 0.189. Read the table as a sensitivity, not a model selection: report the range of status across the domes the data cannot reject. With a tail cut the scenarios differ less, because the bins where the dome acts are excluded:

fit_cut_sel <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                     settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", tail_cut = 47))
ds_cut <- dome_sens_flicc(fit_cut_sel, gear = "Gillnet", se = FALSE)
data.frame(scenario = ds$table$scenario, SPR_no_cut = ds$table$SPR_last,
           SPR_cut47 = ds_cut$table$SPR_last)
#>   scenario SPR_no_cut SPR_cut47
#> 1     base      0.166     0.247
#> 2  rsd1000      0.165     0.265
#> 3  rsd47.3      0.169     0.274
#> 4    rsd39      0.171     0.279
#> 5  rsd30.6      0.176     0.288
#> 6  rsd22.3      0.189     0.310

Here the cut narrows the range across no to moderate doming from 0.165-0.189 to 0.265-0.31.

Integrating the dome levels. Instead of reporting the dome levels side by side, they can be combined into one estimate with ensemble_flicc(). For each year the ensemble is the mixture of the members’ distributions of log SPR, ∑iwiN(μi,sei2)\sum_i w_i\,N(\mu_i, se_i^2); its variance is the within-fit part ∑iwisei2\sum_i w_i se_i^2 plus the between-fit part ∑iwi(μi−μ‾)2\sum_i w_i(\mu_i-\bar\mu)^2, and the median and interval are quantiles of the mixture. Equal weights are the natural choice for assumptions the data cannot distinguish; Akaike weights (weights = "aic") are only allowed when all members use the same data and likelihood, which holds for the dome levels but not, for example, across tail cuts.

ens <- ensemble_flicc(ds$fits[-1])     # the five dome levels, equal weights
ens$members
#>      name weight      AIC dAIC SPR_last se_log_last
#> 1 rsd1000    0.2 74035.05 6.72    0.165       0.115
#> 2 rsd47.3    0.2 74033.75 5.42    0.169       0.118
#> 3   rsd39    0.2 74033.10 4.77    0.171       0.119
#> 4 rsd30.6    0.2 74031.77 3.44    0.176       0.122
#> 5 rsd22.3    0.2 74028.33 0.00    0.189       0.129
tail(ens$table[, c("year", "spr", "lwr", "upr", "sd_within", "sd_between")], 3)
#>    year       spr       lwr       upr sd_within sd_between
#> 10 2022 0.2063425 0.1654505 0.2614319 0.1083785 0.04284013
#> 11 2023 0.2097350 0.1672355 0.2678229 0.1109220 0.04559810
#> 12 2024 0.1734329 0.1358433 0.2256820 0.1207019 0.04620789
plot_ensemble_flicc(ens)

The sensitivity is meant for gears assumed asymptotic. For a gear already fitted as a dome (here the trawl, estimated right-hand SD about 19.4 cm), fixing a wide right-hand SD forces a shape the data reject, which shows as very large dAIC.

7.6 Comparing selectivity functions

plot_compare_sel() draws the fitted selectivity of a list of fits, one panel per gear and one colour per fit. The example refits the reference model with four selectivity functions for the gillnet, keeping the trawl as a double-sided normal: logistic; double-sided normal with the right-hand SD fixed at 1000 (a flat right limb, close to the logistic in shape); normal (a symmetric dome); and double-sided normal with both SDs estimated. The vectors gill_fun and gill_fix hold the gillnet function and the fixed parameters of each run, and Map() fits one model per pair.

gill_fun <- c(logistic = "logistic", dsnormal_rsd1000 = "dsnormal",
              normal = "normal", dsnormal = "dsnormal")
gill_fix <- list(NULL, list(rsd = 1000), NULL, NULL)
fits_sel <- Map(function(fun, fix) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = c("dsnormal", fun), catch_by_gear = cbg,
         sel_fixed = if (is.null(fix)) NULL else list(Gillnet = fix),
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"))
}, gill_fun, gill_fix)
plot_compare_sel(fits_sel)

sel_tab <- data.frame(fit = names(fits_sel),
                      AIC = sapply(fits_sel, function(f) round(AIC(LLflicc(f)), 1)),
                      SPR_last = sapply(fits_sel, function(f) round(sprcur_flicc(f), 3)),
                      row.names = NULL)
sel_tab$dAIC <- sel_tab$AIC - min(sel_tab$AIC)
sel_tab
#>                fit     AIC SPR_last  dAIC
#> 1         logistic 74021.1    0.166  42.5
#> 2 dsnormal_rsd1000 74035.0    0.165  56.4
#> 3           normal 74105.5    0.369 126.9
#> 4         dsnormal 73978.6    0.639   0.0

The trawl panel shows how far the trawl estimate moves when only the gillnet shape changes. Over the four gillnet functions the last-year SPR ranges from 0.165 to 0.639, with dAIC from 0 to 126.9. As with the dome sensitivity, read the comparison together with gear knowledge: a better fit for a dome does not show that large fish are less selected, because a shortage of large fish can also come from F.

7.7 Choosing selectivity

  • Use logistic unless gear knowledge (gillnet mesh, hook size, availability of large fish) supports a dome.
  • A dome fitted without support absorbs a shortage of large fish that may come from F; SPR then becomes optimistic.
  • Several gears sampling different length ranges make domes more identifiable.
  • A tail cut (section Tail of the length composition) reduces the cost of an unmodelled mild dome (simulation: a strong dome fitted as logistic, -17% bias in SPR; with a cut at 0.8 Linf, +1%).
  • Always run the dome sensitivity for gears assumed logistic, and report it.

7.8 Check 6: selectivity plausibility

Look for Ascending limbs consistent with the gear and the left limb of the compositions; domes only where expected.
Red flags Very narrow domes; σR\sigma_R at very small values for a gear expected to be logistic; L50 below the smallest sampled fish.
Action Compare logistic and dome by AIC and by status; fix parameters from external information; use a tail cut.

8 Fitting and fit checks

8.1 The model in brief

For each gear gg and year yy, fishing mortality at length is the gear’s F times its selectivity, Fg,y(L)=Fg,ySg(L)F_{g,y}(L) = F_{g,y}S_g(L), and total mortality is Zy(L)=M(L)+∑gFg,y(L)Z_y(L) = M(L) + \sum_g F_{g,y}(L). Fish grow through the length bins following von Bertalanffy growth, with variation in Linf among fish; the expected length composition of each gear’s catch follows from the numbers surviving to each length and the gear’s F. Each year is fitted as an equilibrium at that year’s F, with F linked between years by a random walk and selectivity shared by all years. Status is the spawning potential ratio, SPRy=∑LNFy(L)W(L)Pmat(L)∑LN0(L)W(L)Pmat(L), \mathrm{SPR}_y = \frac{\sum_L N_{F_y}(L) W(L) P_{mat}(L)}{\sum_L N_0(L) W(L) P_{mat}(L)} , the spawning output per recruit at the year’s F relative to the unfished state. The equations are in section Model equations and comparison of models.

8.2 Fitting the reference model

The reference fit was made in section The reference fit; it takes under a second:

system.time(fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                   settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating")))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    0.37    0.00    0.94
sigmaF_flicc(fit)
#> [1] 0.3
neff_flicc(fit)[1:4, ]
#>    gear year   n   alpha0     neff
#> 1 Trawl 2013 600 790.3777 341.5091
#> 2 Trawl 2014 600 790.3777 341.5091
#> 3 Trawl 2015 600 790.3777 341.5091
#> 4 Trawl 2016 600 790.3777 341.5091

Setting Default Role

8.4 Check 7: convergence

flicc_convergence(fit)
#>                              check              value passed
#> 2           Gradient is acceptable          5.704e-05   TRUE
#> 3     Hessian is positive definite               TRUE   TRUE
#> 4        Standard errors available 31 / 31 parameters   TRUE
#> 5 Hessian eigenvalues are positive              14.22   TRUE
#> 6   Newton decrement is negligible           2.38e-13   TRUE
#> 7                          Overall                 ok   TRUE
#>                                                                                        interpretation
#> 2                                                             The fit is close to a stationary point.
#> 3                                                                The model curvature is well behaved.
#> 4                                                  Uncertainty could be estimated for all parameters.
#> 5                                             No flat or negative curvature directions were detected.

Pass convergence code 0, maximum gradient < 0.001-0.01, positive-definite Hessian, finite standard errors.
Red flags large gradient after restarts; non-positive-definite Hessian; parameters at bounds (F/M at FM_min/FM_max, very small selectivity spreads).
Action more restarts (n_restart); restart from fit$opt$par; simplify selectivity (logistic, fewer gears); check sample sizes; a tail cut or rob_eps if the tail drives the problem.

8.5 Check 8: fit to the compositions

plot_len(fit, by_gear = TRUE, year = 2020:2024)

plot_len(fit)

Look for Predictions through the observed modes and descending limbs in every gear.
Red flags Systematic misfit of the left limb (selectivity), of the tail (Linf, CVL, dome), or of one gear only; the misfit changing sign between periods (time-varying selectivity or sampling).
Action Revisit selectivity form and Linf; tail cut; split periods.

8.6 Residual diagnostics

FLicc is an equilibrium model: each year’s composition is explained by the equilibrium at that year’s F. Strong and weak year classes growing through the compositions are therefore expected to leave patterns in the residuals. The aim of the diagnostics is not to remove these patterns but to see them and judge their size, and to separate them from misfit that a setting can fix (selectivity, Linf, tail, effective sample size).

Residuals. resid_flicc() computes residuals consistent with the likelihood of the fit (effective sample size, observation model, tail cut, plus group):

  • Pearson residuals, r=(o−nπ)/Vr = (o - n\pi)/\sqrt{V}, with V=nπ(1−π)V = n\pi(1-\pi) for the multinomial and the same times (n+α0)/(1+α0)(n+\alpha_0)/(1+\alpha_0) for the Dirichlet-multinomial. They are easy to read in bubble plots but correlated within a composition and not normal for small expected counts.
  • One-step-ahead (OSA) residuals: the composition is split, along increasing length, into a sequence of conditional binomials (beta-binomials for the Dirichlet-multinomial), and each observed count is turned into a randomized quantile residual r=Φ−1(u)r = \Phi^{-1}(u). Under a correct model they are independent standard normal (Trijoulet et al. 2023), so QQ plots and tests are valid.

How OSA residuals work. A composition is not a set of independent numbers: with nn fish measured, a high count in one bin forces lower counts elsewhere. OSA residuals step through the bins of one composition, from small to large, and ask at each step a conditional question:

  • bin 1: of all nn fish, how many should be in bin 1? Binomial(n,π1)(n, \pi_1);
  • bin 2: of the fish not in bin 1, how many should be in bin 2? Binomial(n−o1,π2/(1−π1))(n - o_1, \pi_2/(1-\pi_1)); and so on. The last bin is determined by the others and has no residual.

The observed count is located in its predicted distribution: at the 97.5th percentile, u=0.975u = 0.975 and r=Φ−1(0.975)=1.96r = \Phi^{-1}(0.975) = 1.96. Because counts are whole numbers, uu is drawn at random within the step of the distribution where the count falls (the “randomized” part). For the Dirichlet-multinomial the binomials are beta-binomials, so its extra variance is included.

“One step ahead” refers to stepping through the bins, not through time. In models with random effects, OSA residuals step through time and re-estimate the random effects at each step. FLicc has no random effects by default (F is estimated each year, the random walk is a penalty), so the expected compositions are fixed once the model is fitted and the residuals are exact and cheap.

Reading them:

  • Size: about 5% beyond ±2\pm 2, almost none beyond ±3\pm 3.
  • Sign: each residual is conditional on the smaller bins. A positive residual at length LL means that, of the fish still present at LL or larger, more were in bin LL than predicted: fish “drop out” faster than the model expects (higher mortality or falling selectivity), as in a catch curve. A negative residual means more fish carried on to larger sizes.
  • Spread: an sd well above 1 means the data are noisier than the effective sample size and observation model allow (intervals too narrow); well below 1, that the noise is overstated.
  • Process variation: the model does not include year-class strength, so strong and weak year classes appear as structure in the residuals (runs along the cohort tracks, mean-length runs) rather than as noise.
  • Few data per parameter: residuals are computed at parameters estimated from the same data, so they shrink towards zero (sd below 1) when there are few data per parameter, e.g. a fit to a single year. A single year also gives no between-year diagnostics, and a year-class bump within one composition cannot be told apart from a selectivity misfit at those lengths. Across years, cohorts move along the growth tracks while selectivity misfit stays at the same length; the joint fit with shared selectivity is what lets the residuals separate the two.
res_osa <- resid_flicc(fit, type = "osa")
c(mean = mean(res_osa$resid, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(res_osa$resid, na.rm = TRUE))
#>       mean         sd 
#> 0.05655158 0.99622117
plot_resid_qq(res_osa)

Bubble plots. Residuals by length and year; blue where more fish were observed than expected, red where fewer. cohorts = TRUE adds von Bertalanffy growth tracks of year classes (grey lines):

plot_resid_bubble(res_osa, fit = fit, cohorts = TRUE)

plot_resid_len(fit,years="each")

plot_resid_len(fit,years="each",type="osa")

Mean length and runs test. The observed mean length of each composition is compared with its expectation, standardized with the standard error implied by the observation model (Francis 2011). A runs test checks whether the residuals change sign as often as random residuals would; too few runs mean systematic structure (green background: passed; red: failed; limits at three standard deviations, as in ss3diags and JABBA):

lmr <- lmean_resid_flicc(fit)
lmr$runs
#>            gear p_value pass sd_z
#> Trawl     Trawl   0.409 TRUE 1.29
#> Gillnet Gillnet   0.965 TRUE 1.09
lmr$plot

Posterior predictive checks. ppc_flicc() simulates compositions from the fitted model (at the effective sample size and with the observation model of the fit) and compares observed statistics with their predictive distribution: mean length, 95th percentile, proportion of mature fish and largest length. With par_draws = TRUE the parameters are also drawn from their estimated uncertainty.

ppc <- ppc_flicc(fit, nsim = 300)
ppc$coverage
#>      gear  stat share_outside_95
#> 1   Trawl Lmean             0.08
#> 2 Gillnet Lmean             0.08
#> 3   Trawl   L95             0.08
#> 4 Gillnet   L95             0.08
#> 5   Trawl  Pmat             0.08
#> 6 Gillnet  Pmat             0.00
#> 7   Trawl  Lmax             0.00
#> 8 Gillnet  Lmax             0.25
ppc$plot

In this fit the OSA residuals have sd 1, so the bin-to-bin noise within a year is close to what the observation model allows. The mean lengths, however, vary between years with an sd of 1.29 (trawl) and 1.09 (gillnet) in standardized units, and 8% and 8% of the observed mean lengths lie outside their 95% predictive intervals. Where the between-year variation is large while the within-year noise is not, the misfit is not sampling noise: whole compositions shift between years, as year classes pass through, which the equilibrium model cannot follow.

About 5% of the observed values should lie outside the 95% intervals. Many more means that the effective sample size or the observation model understate the variability of the data, so the intervals of the assessment are too narrow; far fewer means the effective sample size could be higher.

Pattern Likely cause Response
Diagonal runs of one sign along the cohort tracks; mean-length runs test failed strong or weak year classes (expected in an equilibrium model) report it; check that status is robust (retrospective, tail cut); do not over-fit
Vertical bands of one sign at the same lengths in all years selectivity shape logistic vs dome; dome sensitivity
Misfit of the largest fish in all years Linf, CVL or doming Linf sensitivity, tail cut
A change of sign between periods change of selectivity, gear or sampling split periods; by_year check
Many observed statistics outside the predictive intervals ESS too high, or observation model too narrow lower ESS; Dirichlet-multinomial
OSA residuals with sd well above 1 the same the same

8.7 Check 9: retrospective consistency

The model is refitted with the last one, two and three years removed (peels); Map() runs one fit per peel. Mohn’s rho compares the terminal SPR of each peel with the SPR of the same year in the full fit.

yrs <- as.numeric(dimnames(lfd[[1]])$year)
peels <- 1:3

retro <- Map(function(p) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"),
         years = head(yrs, -p), se = FALSE)
}, peels)
names(retro) <- paste0("peel", peels)
plot_spr(c(list(full = fit), retro))


spr_full <- c(fit$report$spr)
spr_peel <- sapply(retro, sprcur_flicc)               # terminal SPR of each peel
spr_same <- spr_full[length(spr_full) - peels]        # same years in the full fit
mohn_rho <- mean((spr_peel - spr_same) / spr_same)
round(mohn_rho, 3)
#> [1] 0.034
Pass Mohn’s rho for SPR within about ±0.2.
Red flags Consistent revisions in one direction (the terminal SPR is systematically revised up or down).
Action Check for trends in selectivity or sampling; in a rebuild, an equilibrium model is expected to under-estimate SPR at the end of the series (section Lag under changing F).

9 Reference points and status

9.1 Fspr

The fit stores Fspr for settings$spr_ref (default 40%), computed in TMB:

fspr_flicc(fit)                 # stored Fspr40
#> [1] 0.08997666
fspr_flicc(fit, spr = 30)       # computed
#> [1] 0.1219798
fcur_flicc(fit); sprcur_flicc(fit)
#> [1] 0.1949528
#> [1] 0.1660614

9.2 Equilibrium curves and MSY proxies

eqstklen() computes equilibrium per-recruit quantities over a range of F at the fitted selectivity (mean of the last nyears), and converts them with steepness s to equilibrium SSB, recruitment and yield under Beverton-Holt: RR0=4sSPR(F)−(1−s)(5s−1)SPR(F),Y(F)=YPR(F)R(F),B(F)=SBPR(F)R(F). \frac{R}{R_0} = \frac{4s\,\mathrm{SPR}(F) - (1-s)}{(5s-1)\,\mathrm{SPR}(F)}, \qquad Y(F) = \mathrm{YPR}(F)\, R(F), \qquad B(F) = \mathrm{SBPR}(F)\, R(F). @refpts lists the reference points derived from these curves (F and the equilibrium quantities at the SPR target and at maximum yield).

eqstk <- eqstklen(fit, s = 0.75)
eqstk@refpts
#> An object of class "FLPar"
#> params
#>   Fcur   Fspr   Ycur SSBcur SPRcur   SPR0 
#> 0.1950 0.0900 0.7250 0.0902 0.1661 3.0220 
#> units:  NA
plot_eqcurves(eqstk)

The same quantities without steepness, as per-recruit curves:

prbrp <- prbrp_flicc(fit)
fmsy_flicc(prbrp, s = 0.75)
#> [1] 0.1053
fspr_flicc(fit, spr = 35)
#> [1] 0.1045769

9.3 From SPR to relative spawning biomass

With Beverton-Holt recruitment of steepness ss, BB0=4sSPR−(1−s)5s−1,BBtgt=4sSPR−(1−s)4sSPRtgt−(1−s), \frac{B}{B_0} = \frac{4s\,\mathrm{SPR} - (1 - s)}{5s - 1}, \qquad \frac{B}{B_{tgt}} = \frac{4s\,\mathrm{SPR} - (1-s)}{4s\,\mathrm{SPR}_{tgt} - (1-s)} , so SPR overstates depletion when s<1s < 1. spr2brel() and flicc2FLStockR(s = ) apply the mapping (F is unchanged):

round(spr2brel(c(0.2, 0.3, 0.4), s = 0.75, sprref = 40), 3)
#> [1] 0.368 0.684 1.000
plot_LBAdvice(FLStocks(SPR = flicc2FLStockR(fit, rel = TRUE),
                       relB_s0.75 = flicc2FLStockR(fit, rel = TRUE, s = 0.75)), panel = 1)

9.4 Stock status and advice plots

plot_spr() shows the SPR trajectory with its interval, and plot_lbfao() the same against the FAO status bands (overfished below the SPR target, sustainable above):

plot_spr(fit, ci = TRUE)

plot_lbfao(fit)

flicc2FLStockR() converts the fit into an FLStockR object for advice plots: SPR (or B/BtgtB/B_{tgt} with s) as the biomass indicator and F relative to Fspr, with reference points from the SPR target (spr.btgt = 0.4), bpa and blim:

stk <- flicc2FLStockR(fit)
stk@refpts
#> An object of class "FLPar"
#> params
#> Fspr Bspr  Bpa Blim 
#> 0.09 0.40 0.20 0.10 
#> units:  NA
plot_LBAdvice(stk)

With rel = TRUE the indicators are relative to the target (1 = at target), the usual form for advice:

stk_rel <- flicc2FLStockR(fit, rel = TRUE)
plot_LBAdvice(stk_rel, panels = 1) + ylim(0, 1.5)

flicc_stklen(fit) returns the fitted FLStockLen (numbers, catch and F at length by year) for further FLR workflows.

9.5 Status over F, selectivity and gear shares: contour plots

contour_flicc() computes yield per recruit and SPR over a grid, and plot_contour_flicc() draws one row per gear with yield on the left and spawning potential on the right. The grid can be laid out in three ways (view):

view x-axis y-axis other gears
"fleet" (default) total F, F shares between gears as now the gear’s SL50 (logistic) or mode (dome) F scaled with the total, selectivity as fitted
"share" total F the gear’s share of the total F (%) the rest of the total F, in their current proportions
"gear" the gear’s own F the gear’s SL50 or mode current F and selectivity

A change of selectivity shifts the gear’s curve along the length axis, keeping its shape. Yield is shown as % of its maximum over the grid (viridis colours); SPR in % on a scale anchored on the reference points: red below SPR 20%, orange to pale yellow between 20% and 40%, blue above 40%. The black lines are SPR 40% (solid) and 20% (dashed), the point is the current state, and the dotted horizontal line is the length at 50% maturity (Lmat).

The default view asks: if the whole fleet fished more or less, with the gears in their current proportions, and one gear changed its selectivity, what would yield and SPR be?

cf <- contour_flicc(fit)
cf$current
#>            gear     type      loc         F       SPR       YPR    YPRrel
#> Trawl     Trawl dsnormal 23.83475 0.2107964 0.1660614 0.1470791 0.8569229
#> Gillnet Gillnet logistic 30.35835 0.2107964 0.1660614 0.1470791 1.0001515
#>             Fshare     Cshare
#> Trawl   0.92103616 0.94969439
#> Gillnet 0.07896384 0.05030561
plot_contour_flicc(cf)

The share view keeps all selectivities as fitted and asks how the split of F between gears matters. With two gears the two rows mirror each other, so one gear is enough. The subtitle gives the gear’s current share of F and of the catch; the two differ because the gears catch fish of different sizes.

cs <- contour_flicc(fit, view = "share", gear = "Gillnet")
plot_contour_flicc(cs)

In the "gear" view only one gear’s F changes; the other gears keep fishing at their current F, so at zero F of one gear the SPR reflects the other gear alone, and the catch split changes along the axis.

Per-recruit results assume constant recruitment. With a steepness s, the same surfaces are converted under a Beverton-Holt relationship to SSB% (spawning biomass in % of unfished, B/B0B/B_0) and Yield% (equilibrium yield in % of its maximum over the grid), with R/R0=4sSPR−(1−s)(5s−1)SPRR/R_0 = \frac{4s\,SPR - (1-s)}{(5s-1)\,SPR} and B/B0=4sSPR−(1−s)5s−1B/B_0 = \frac{4s\,SPR - (1-s)}{5s-1}. The black lines are then SSB 40% and 20%:

plot_contour_flicc(cf, s = 0.75)

How to read them:

  • Moving left (less F) or up (larger fish first caught) raises SPR; the yield isopleths show what that costs, or gains.
  • Here the gillnet catches at SL50 = 30.4 cm, below Lmat (31.2 cm). With all F as now, raising the gillnet SL50 to Lmat gives an SPR of about 17% (now 17%) for a change in YPR of 0%; reaching SPR 40% at the current SL50 by the gillnet alone needs its F cut by about more than 100%.
  • Without s the surfaces are per-recruit results; with s they include the loss of recruitment at low spawning biomass, so yield falls off more steeply at high F. Both are equilibrium results at the fitted life history, a guide to direction and scale, not a forecast.

gear = selects gears (rows), n the grid resolution, Fmax and Lrange the axes, ref the reference levels (target, limit), and levels, ylevels the grey isopleths of the two columns.

10 Sensitivity runs and ensembles: a single year

Many assessments have length data for one year only. FLicc then fits that year (years =), and the uncertainty about the assumptions comes from sensitivity runs: the same data refitted with one assumption changed at a time. fits_summary() gives one table for a list of fits, and ensemble_flicc() combines them into one estimate of SPR.

The reference fit and the sensitivity runs for the last year of the alfonsino data: the gillnet with a dome (right-hand SD fixed at 0.85, 0.7 and 0.55 x Linf), CVL 0.08 and 0.12, and Linf +/- 10%. lapply() runs one fit per value. The upper bound of apical F/M is raised from its default (FM_max = 4) to 10, so that runs with a larger Linf can reach a higher F:

yr <- 2024
set_ref <- list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "mn", FM_max = 4)

fit1 <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
               settings = set_ref, years = yr)

rsd <- c(dome_0.85 = 47, dome_0.7 = 39, dome_0.55 = 31)       # x Linf = 55.7
dome_runs <- lapply(rsd, function(r)
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = c("dsnormal", "dsnormal"), catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = set_ref, years = yr, sel_fixed = list(Gillnet = list(rsd = r))))

cvl <- c(CVL_0.08 = 0.08, CVL_0.12 = 0.12)
cvl_runs <- lapply(cvl, function(cv)
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = modifyList(set_ref, list(CVL = cv)), years = yr))

linf <- c(Linf_50 = 50.1, Linf_61 = 61.3)
linf_runs <- lapply(linf, function(li) {
  lh <- lhpar; lh["linf"] <- li
  fiticc(lfd, stocklen(lfd, lh, m_model = "constant"), sel_fun = sel_fun,
         catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = set_ref, years = yr)
})

runs1 <- c(list(reference = fit1), dome_runs, cvl_runs, linf_runs)
tab1 <- fits_summary(runs1)
tab1
#>         run conv   SPR   lwr   upr    FM   Fap Fspr40 F_Fspr40    AIC dAIC
#> 1 reference   ok 0.136 0.109 0.170 1.352 0.219  0.082    2.669 6260.0  0.0
#> 2 dome_0.85   ok 0.145 0.115 0.184 1.273 0.206  0.081    2.541 6266.7  6.7
#> 3  dome_0.7   ok 0.146 0.115 0.185 1.269 0.206  0.081    2.533 6266.7  6.7
#> 4 dome_0.55   ok 0.147 0.116 0.187 1.261 0.204  0.081    2.518 6266.6  6.7
#> 5  CVL_0.08   ok 0.145 0.116 0.180 1.281 0.207  0.081    2.551 6257.9 -2.1
#> 6  CVL_0.12   ok 0.125 0.094 0.167 1.467 0.238  0.083    2.850 6263.0  3.0
#> 7   Linf_50   ok 0.260 0.209 0.324 0.775 0.126  0.079    1.585 6253.6 -6.4
#> 8   Linf_61   ok 0.078 0.062 0.098 2.078 0.337  0.086    3.934 6264.6  4.6

Residual options for single year fits.

plot_resid_len(fit1,type="pearson")

plot_resid_len(fit1,type="osa")

fits_summary() gives, for each run, the convergence (conv), SPR with its confidence interval, F/M, apical F, Fspr40, current F relative to Fspr40, and AIC with dAIC relative to the first run. Use only runs with conv = "ok": a run that fails is not a result (a typical failure: F slides to the lower bound of F/M and SPR to almost 1, i.e. the composition is explained without fishing). Here all runs converged. AIC is comparable between the runs because all use the same data and likelihood; a change of data (e.g. a tail cut, another ESS) breaks this.

Two ensembles of the converged runs: equal weights, and Akaike weights:

ok1 <- runs1[tab1$conv == "ok"]

ens_eq  <- ensemble_flicc(ok1, weights = "equal")
ens_aic <- ensemble_flicc(ok1, weights = "aic")
ens_eq$members
#>        name weight     AIC  dAIC SPR_last se_log_last
#> 1 reference  0.125 6259.97  6.37    0.136       0.112
#> 2 dome_0.85  0.125 6266.69 13.09    0.145       0.121
#> 3  dome_0.7  0.125 6266.67 13.07    0.146       0.121
#> 4 dome_0.55  0.125 6266.63 13.03    0.147       0.123
#> 5  CVL_0.08  0.125 6257.87  4.27    0.145       0.112
#> 6  CVL_0.12  0.125 6263.02  9.42    0.125       0.146
#> 7   Linf_50  0.125 6253.60  0.00    0.260       0.112
#> 8   Linf_61  0.125 6264.58 10.98    0.078       0.116
ens_aic$members
#>        name weight     AIC  dAIC SPR_last se_log_last
#> 1 reference  0.035 6259.97  6.37    0.136       0.112
#> 2 dome_0.85  0.001 6266.69 13.09    0.145       0.121
#> 3  dome_0.7  0.001 6266.67 13.07    0.146       0.121
#> 4 dome_0.55  0.001 6266.63 13.03    0.147       0.123
#> 5  CVL_0.08  0.100 6257.87  4.27    0.145       0.112
#> 6  CVL_0.12  0.008 6263.02  9.42    0.125       0.146
#> 7   Linf_50  0.850 6253.60  0.00    0.260       0.112
#> 8   Linf_61  0.004 6264.58 10.98    0.078       0.116
rbind(equal = ens_eq$table, aic = ens_aic$table)[, c("year", "spr", "lwr", "upr", "sd_within", "sd_between")]
#>       year       spr        lwr       upr sd_within sd_between
#> equal 2024 0.1412501 0.07075546 0.2856443 0.1210167  0.3050354
#> aic   2024 0.2535648 0.12499338 0.3211638 0.1122987  0.2251432
plot_ensemble_flicc(ens_eq)

plot_ensemble_flicc(ens_aic)

With one year, plot_ensemble_flicc() shows each member and the ensemble as a point with its interval. The two weightings answer different questions:

  • Equal weights treat the runs as assumptions the data cannot decide between (a dome, Linf, CVL): the ensemble interval adds the spread between the runs (sd_between) to the uncertainty within each fit (sd_within). This is the usual choice for structural uncertainty.
  • Akaike weights let the data decide. Here the AIC differences are small (at most 13.1), so the weights spread over the runs and favour the domes. With large samples (many fish, or an ESS of 500 per gear) AIC differences of 10 or more are common, and the best run then takes almost all the weight: the ensemble becomes a model selection. Use it as a check, and only for runs with the same data and likelihood. Linf in particular is informed mainly by the few largest fish, so AIC weights over Linf follow the tail of the composition rather than growth studies.

The same functions work for several years and for the dome levels of dome_sens_flicc() (section Dome sensitivity).

One fleet with two size modes. When catch shares by gear are uncertain, or for a quick single-fleet assessment, the gears can be pooled with combine_lfd() (section Exploring selectivity shapes) and fitted as one fleet. Its selectivity then has to describe both modes. The runs: logistic, "binormal", "bidsnormal", and "bidsnormal" with a flat second mode (rsd2 = 1000 fixed). The pooled composition is rescaled to an ESS of 500 and shows no overdispersion beyond it, so the Dirichlet-multinomial precision is fixed (dm_theta = "fixed"); estimated, it runs to its upper bound and the fits fail the convergence check:


fit2gear <-fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
              settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"))

lfd_fleet <- combine_lfd(lfd, catch_by_gear = c(0.95,0.05) ,
                         lhpar = lhpar, ess.n = 500)


stk_fleet <- stocklen(lfd_fleet, lhpar, m_model = "constant")




fleet_fun <- c(logistic = "logistic", binormal = "binormal",
               bidsnormal = "bidsnormal", bidsnormal_flat = "bidsnormal")
fleet_fix <- list(NULL, NULL, NULL, list(fleet = list(rsd2 = 1000)))

set_fleet <- modifyList(set_ref, list(dm_theta = "fixed"))

fleet_runs <- Map(function(fun, fix) {
  fiticc(lfd_fleet, stk_fleet, sel_fun = fun, catch_by_gear = 1,
         settings = set_fleet, sel_fixed = fix)
}, fleet_fun, fleet_fix)

tab_fleet <- fits_summary(c(list(ref2gear=fit2gear),fleet_runs))
tab_fleet
#>               run conv   SPR   lwr   upr    FM   Fap Fspr40 F_Fspr40     AIC
#> 1        ref2gear   ok 0.166 0.133 0.207 1.203 0.195  0.090    2.167 74021.1
#> 2        logistic   ok 0.162 0.129 0.204 1.130 0.183  0.079    2.330 36564.7
#> 3        binormal   ok 0.295 0.188 0.463 0.965 0.156  0.115    1.361 36578.5
#> 4      bidsnormal   ok 0.380 0.218 0.662 0.776 0.126  0.119    1.060 36517.6
#> 5 bidsnormal_flat   ok 0.139 0.110 0.175 1.369 0.222  0.084    2.649 36527.3
#>       dAIC
#> 1      0.0
#> 2 -37456.4
#> 3 -37442.6
#> 4 -37503.5
#> 5 -37493.9
plot_compare_sel(fleet_runs)

ok_fleet   <- tab_fleet$conv == "ok"
best_fleet <- if (any(ok_fleet)) tab_fleet$run[ok_fleet][which.min(tab_fleet$AIC[ok_fleet])] else
  tab_fleet$run[which.min(tab_fleet$AIC)]
best_fleet
#> [1] "bidsnormal"
plot_len(fleet_runs[[best_fleet]])

selpars_flicc(fleet_runs$bidsnormal)
#> An object of class "FLPars"
#> [[1]]
#> An object of class "FLPar"
#> params
#> mode1   sd1 mode2  lsd2  rsd2     h 
#> 22.80  3.00 29.53  3.01  8.97  1.23 
#> units:  cm 
#> 
#> Slot "names":
#> [1] "fleet"
#> 
#> Slot "desc":
#> character(0)
#> 
#> Slot "lock":
#> [1] FALSE
selpars_flicc(fleet_runs$bidsnormal_flat)
#> An object of class "FLPars"
#> [[1]]
#> An object of class "FLPar"
#> params
#>   mode1     sd1   mode2    lsd2    rsd2       h 
#>   22.61    2.96   30.57    3.97 1000.00    1.72 
#> units:  cm 
#> 
#> Slot "names":
#> [1] "fleet"
#> 
#> Slot "desc":
#> character(0)
#> 
#> Slot "lock":
#> [1] FALSE

AIC compares the fleet runs with each other (same pooled data), not with the two-gear runs. A logistic curve cannot follow two modes: it reads the decline after the first mode as fishing mortality. The free "bidsnormal" shows the risk of six parameters on one year of data: its right limb runs to a very large SD (rsd2 of 9 cm), a flat direction of the likelihood, and the fit fails. With rsd2 = 1000 fixed (bidsnormal_flat) the same shape converges: a first mode at about 23 cm and, from about 31 cm, a plateau at the relative height h: the larger fish are retained at a constant, lower level. A near-zero lsd2 (a step up to the plateau instead of a second mode) is typical when the data show no separate second mode; check selpars_flicc() and plot_compare_sel() before using a two-mode fit. "binormal" converges, but its SPR interval is wide.

SPR of the pooled runs spans 0.139 to 0.38, against 0.136 for the two-gear reference: with one fleet, the selectivity curve and F share the information in one composition, and the shape chosen for the large-fish mode decides how much of the decline is attributed to fishing. The two-gear fit is preferable where the catch shares are known: it keeps the selectivity of each gear, while pooling assumes that each gear’s sample represents its catch.

11 Length-based indicators

11.1 LBIspr

For each gear, LBIspr() compares the observed proportion of large fish with the proportion expected at the reference FSPRxF_{\mathrm{SPR}x}:

  1. Equilibrium numbers-at-length at FSPRxF_{\mathrm{SPR}x}, Nref(L)N^{ref}(L), and the reference catch composition of gear gg, vg(L)=Nref(L)Sg(L)v_g(L) = N^{ref}(L) S_g(L) (retained bins only, i.e. below the tail cut).
  2. Threshold length Lg*L^*_g: the length at which the cumulative vgv_g reaches the fraction thresh (default 0.75) of its total.
  3. Reference proportion above the threshold, Pgref=∑L≥Lg*vg(L)/∑Lvg(L)P^{ref}_g = \sum_{L \ge L^*_g} v_g(L) / \sum_L v_g(L) (about 1−1 - thresh).
  4. Observed proportion in year yy, Pg,yobs=∑L≥Lg*yg,y,L/∑Lyg,y,LP^{obs}_{g,y} = \sum_{L \ge L^*_g} y_{g,y,L} / \sum_L y_{g,y,L}.
  5. Indicator LBIg,y=Pg,yobs/Pgref\mathrm{LBI}_{g,y} = P^{obs}_{g,y}/P^{ref}_g.

LBI=1\mathrm{LBI} = 1: as many large fish as at the target; <1< 1: fewer, i.e. F above FSPRxF_{\mathrm{SPR}x}. The threshold lengths are returned as attr(, "Lref").

lbi <- LBIspr(fit, spr = 40, thresh = 0.75)
attr(lbi, "Lref")
#>   Trawl Gillnet 
#>      30      39
plot_LBIspr(fit, thresh = 0.75)

plot_LBIp(fit, year = 2024)

11.2 LBImean

LBImean() is the model-based analogue of the ICES mean-length indicator L‾/LF=M\bar L/L_{F=M}: the reference mean length (above lc, default the gear’s 50% selectivity length) is computed from the fitted model at F=MF = M (ref = "FM") or at FSPRxF_{\mathrm{SPR}x} (ref = "spr"), using the fitted growth variability and gear selectivity, including domes.

LBImean(fit, ref = "FM")
