11.3 Indicators and the tail cut

Both indicators use the fit’s tail cut by default (tail_cut = NULL), so the indicator and the likelihood use the same bins; tail_cut = FALSE uses all bins.

11.4 Check 10: indicators against status

Look for LBIspr and SPR/SPR40 telling the same story; similar indicators across gears.
Red flags Gears disagreeing strongly (selectivity misfit or sampling); indicator noise much larger than the SPR trend.
Action Use the more informative gear; pool gears (pool in flicc.sa()); smooth in the harvest control rule.

Part II: Technical options

12 Effective sample size and observation models

12.1 How the sample size enters the likelihood

For gear gg in year yy, with observed counts yg,y,ly_{g,y,l}, total ng,y=∑lyg,y,ln_{g,y} = \sum_l y_{g,y,l} and predicted proportions πg,y,l\pi_{g,y,l}:

  • Multinomial (obs_model = "mn"): −logL=−∑lyg,y,llogπg,y,l-\log L = -\sum_l y_{g,y,l} \log \pi_{g,y,l}. The weight of a composition is proportional to ng,yn_{g,y}.
  • Negative binomial ("nb"): counts with mean ng,yπg,y,ln_{g,y}\pi_{g,y,l} and overdispersion ϕ\phi (estimated), variance μ+μ2/ϕ\mu + \mu^2/\phi.
  • Dirichlet-multinomial ("dm"): the compositions are drawn from a Dirichlet with mean πg,y\pi_{g,y} and precision α0\alpha_0; in FLicc α0=ng,y\alpha_0 = n_{g,y}. The variance of the proportions is inflated by (n+α0)/(1+α0)≈2(n + \alpha_0)/(1 + \alpha_0) \approx 2, so a DM fit at sample size nn carries about the information of a multinomial with n/2n/2. Its log-gamma form also penalises single-bin misfits less than the multinomial, which makes it more robust with messy real data.

lfdess(lfd, ess.g) rescales each gear-year to the given effective sample size (ESS), keeping the proportions; empty gear-years stay empty.

12.2 Why very large sample sizes do harm

Measured fish are not independent: fish from one haul or trip share its length structure. Raw counts (often thousands) therefore overstate the information by an order of magnitude. With an overstated sample size:

  • the likelihood is dominated by small structural misfits (growth model, binning, selectivity shape) rather than the signal, so estimates and their standard errors are overconfident;
  • log-likelihood differences between alternative assumptions become huge, so AIC weights across an ensemble collapse onto a few draws and likelihood profiles become jagged or multimodal;
  • any discrete effect (a fish entering or leaving the range of the largest growth group) is multiplied by nn.

12.3 Choosing the effective sample size

With the default likelihood (Dirichlet-multinomial with estimated precision, next section) the data choose their own weight: give it the raw counts or an ESS of at least 500 per gear-year, not a reduced ESS. FLicc prints a message when the median sample size is below 500.

The choice of ESS matters for the likelihoods with a weight set by the input, the multinomial (as LBSPR) and the Dirichlet-multinomial with fixed precision (dm_theta = "fixed", as LBB). For these, ESS of about 150-200 per gear-year has given the most stable assessments and ensemble profiles, and 1000 or more behaved poorly in Monte-Carlo profiling:

  • Base ESS on the number of independent sampling units (trips, hauls, vessels) where known, e.g. a few fish-equivalents per unit; otherwise start at 150-200 per gear-year and test 100 and 300.
  • Use the same ESS for gears of similar sampling quality; reduce it for gears with few trips.
  • The fixed Dirichlet-multinomial halves the nominal ESS.
  • Never fit raw counts of several thousand fish per year without rescaling.

The demonstration below shows why the input matters for these likelihoods: it fits the alfonsino data at five effective sample sizes (ess_values), once with the multinomial and once with the fixed Dirichlet-multinomial, and once more with the raw counts. lfdess() rescales the compositions to the given ESS; Map() runs one fit per value. For each fit the table shows the last-year SPR (sprcur_flicc()), its standard error on the log scale (from spr_ci_flicc()) and the largest absolute gradient at the optimum.

sel_fun <- c("dsnormal", "logistic")
cbg <- c(0.95, 0.05)
stklen <- stocklen(lfd, lhpar, m_model = "constant")

ess_values <- c(50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)

# multinomial: one fit per ESS
fits_mn <- Map(function(ess) {
  fiticc(lfdess(lfd, ess.g = ess), stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "mn"))
}, ess_values)
names(fits_mn) <- paste0("mn_", ess_values)

# Dirichlet-multinomial with fixed precision: one fit per ESS
fits_dm <- Map(function(ess) {
  fiticc(lfdess(lfd, ess.g = ess), stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "fixed"))
}, ess_values)
names(fits_dm) <- paste0("dm_", ess_values)

# raw counts (no rescaling)
fit_raw_mn <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                     settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "mn"))
fit_raw_dm <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                     settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "fixed"))
raw_n <- round(mean(quantSums(lfd[["Trawl"]])))   # fish per year, trawl

fits_mn <- c(fits_mn, raw = list(fit_raw_mn))
fits_dm <- c(fits_dm, raw = list(fit_raw_dm))

# standard error of log SPR in the last year
se_logspr <- function(fit) tail(spr_ci_flicc(fit)$se_log, 1)
ess_table <- data.frame(
  ESS        = c(ess_values, paste0("raw (~", raw_n, ")")),
  SPR_mn     = round(sapply(fits_mn, sprcur_flicc), 3),
  SPR_dm     = round(sapply(fits_dm, sprcur_flicc), 3),
  se_mn      = round(sapply(fits_mn, se_logspr), 3),
  se_dm      = round(sapply(fits_dm, se_logspr), 3),
  maxgrad_dm = signif(sapply(fits_dm, function(fit) fit$max_gradient), 2),
  row.names  = NULL)
ess_table
#>          ESS SPR_mn SPR_dm se_mn se_dm maxgrad_dm
#> 1         50  0.173  0.358 0.238 0.236    2.7e-06
#> 2        100  0.171  0.258 0.184 0.205    5.8e-06
#> 3        200  0.167  0.201 0.139 0.167    5.3e-06
#> 4        500  0.163  0.164 0.092 0.118    3.0e-05
#> 5       1000  0.161  0.150 0.066 0.088    2.5e-05
#> 6 raw (~600)  0.174  0.173 0.095 0.123    1.8e-05

Three things change with the effective sample size:

  • Precision: the standard error of log SPR shrinks roughly with 1/n1/\sqrt{n}; with large ESS the intervals reflect the sampling of individual fish, not of the fishery.
  • Convergence: the maximum gradient grows at large ESS (here up to 2.5^{-5} at ESS 1000 with dm), a sign that the likelihood surface becomes sharp and ragged.
  • The estimate itself, for dm: with the multinomial the last-year SPR changes little (0.161 to 0.174), but with the Dirichlet-multinomial it ranges from 0.358 at ESS 50 to 0.15 at ESS 1000. At low ESS the compositions carry little weight against the random walk and the catch-share constraint; estimates stabilise from about ESS 150-200 upward.

The alfonsino example has about 600 fish per gear-year, so its raw counts are moderate; with the thousands of fish per year common in market sampling the effects above are much stronger, also for the AIC weights of a Monte-Carlo ensemble.

SPR with 95% intervals for the Dirichlet-multinomial at ESS 50, 200 and 1000 and for the raw counts:

plot_spr(fits_dm[c("dm_50", "dm_200", "dm_1000", "raw")], ci = TRUE)

12.4 Letting the data choose their weight: estimated Dirichlet-multinomial precision

With dm_theta = "fixed" the Dirichlet precision is α0=n\alpha_0 = n, so the effective sample size the likelihood uses is neff=n(1+α0)n+α0=1+n2≈n2, n_{eff} = \frac{n\,(1 + \alpha_0)}{n + \alpha_0} = \frac{1 + n}{2} \approx \frac{n}{2}, proportional to the input ESS, as shown above. FLicc can instead estimate the precision by gear (Thorson et al. 2017):

dm_theta α0\alpha_0 neffn_{eff} as the input ESS grows
"fixed" nn ≈n/2\approx n/2 grows without limit
"linear" θn\theta n, θ\theta estimated (1+θn)/(1+θ)(1 + \theta n)/(1 + \theta) grows, at a rate set by θ\theta
"saturating" (default) β\beta, estimated n(1+β)/(n+β)n(1 + \beta)/(n + \beta) levels off at β+1\beta + 1

With "saturating", once the input sample size is well above β\beta the effective sample size no longer depends on it: the data estimate how much each composition can count. The input matters only if it is below what the data support. Then there is no overdispersion to estimate, β\beta runs towards infinity, and the model becomes a multinomial at the input sample size; a weak prior (dm_prior_sd = 1, centred close to a multinomial) keeps it finite, and FLicc reports the precision as being at its bound. For this reason, with an estimated precision use the raw counts or an ESS of at least 500, so that the data, not the input, set the weight.

The fits below use the saturating Dirichlet-multinomial at ESS 500 and 1000 and on the raw counts; neff_flicc() reports the estimated effective sample size by gear and year.

dm_inputs <- list(ESS_500 = lfdess(lfd, ess.g = 500), ESS_1000 = lfdess(lfd, ess.g = 1000), raw = lfd)
fits_dms <- Map(function(d) {
  fiticc(d, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"))
}, dm_inputs)

neff_gear <- function(fit, g) { ne <- neff_flicc(fit); round(mean(ne$neff[ne$gear == g])) }
dm_table <- data.frame(
  input        = names(fits_dms),
  SPR_last     = round(sapply(fits_dms, sprcur_flicc), 3),
  se_log       = round(sapply(fits_dms, se_logspr), 3),
  neff_Trawl   = sapply(fits_dms, neff_gear, g = "Trawl"),
  neff_Gillnet = sapply(fits_dms, neff_gear, g = "Gillnet"),
  row.names = NULL)
dm_table
#>      input SPR_last se_log neff_Trawl neff_Gillnet
#> 1  ESS_500    0.165  0.112        351          275
#> 2 ESS_1000    0.156  0.111        314          248
#> 3      raw    0.166  0.113        342          284
plot_spr(c(fixed_ESS_200 = list(fits_dm$dm_200), fits_dms), ci = TRUE)

The last-year SPR is 0.156 to 0.166 whatever the input, against 0.15 to 0.358 for the fixed precision over ESS 50 to 1000. The compositions support an effective sample size of about 342 (trawl) and 284 (gillnet) fish per year; the fixed precision at ESS 200 used about 100.

The estimated precision describes the noise within compositions. Year classes that shift whole compositions between years are a different kind of misfit, which the residual diagnostics (section Residual diagnostics) show and the precision does not absorb.

13 Fishing mortality over time

Log F by gear follows a random walk, logFg,y=logFg,y−1+εg,y,εg,y∼N(0,σF2). \log F_{g,y} = \log F_{g,y-1} + \varepsilon_{g,y}, \qquad \varepsilon_{g,y} \sim N(0, \sigma_F^2). With selectivity Sg(L)S_g(L) shared by all years, the model is fitted to all compositions at once; the objective is −logL=−∑ylogLy(F⋅,y,S)−∑g,y>1logϕ(logFg,y−logFg,y−1;0,σF). -\log L = -\sum_{y} \log L_y\!\left(F_{\cdot,y}, S\right) - \sum_{g,y>1} \log \phi\!\left(\log F_{g,y} - \log F_{g,y-1};\, 0, \sigma_F\right). Compared with fitting each year on its own (as LBSPR does), this has four advantages:

  • Selectivity from all years. The left limb of the compositions is informed by every year, so selectivity is better determined and does not absorb year-to-year sampling noise.
  • Borrowing strength. A year with few fish is fitted close to its neighbours instead of producing an extreme F.
  • Missing years. A year without data of a gear still gets an F, bridged by the random walk (section Missing data).
  • Separation of signal and noise. σF\sigma_F sets how much of the year-to-year change in the compositions is read as a change in F.

The price is smoothing: with small σF\sigma_F a real change in F is spread over several years (section Lag under changing F). The options below differ in how σF\sigma_F is treated.

The four options for σF\sigma_F are fitted below to the same data (raw counts, Dirichlet-multinomial with estimated precision). Only the F settings differ, so each option has its own settings list; Map() fits them in turn.

f_settings <- list(
  fixed_0.3 = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", sigmaF = 0.3),                       # default
  prior     = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", prior_sigmaF = c(log(0.5), 0.3, 1)), # penalised
  F_re      = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", F_re = TRUE),                        # random effects
  no_RW     = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", prior_sigmaF = FALSE))               # no random walk

fits_F <- Map(function(set) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = set)
}, f_settings)

data.frame(option   = names(fits_F),
           sigmaF   = round(sapply(fits_F, sigmaF_flicc), 3),
           SPR_last = round(sapply(fits_F, sprcur_flicc), 3),
           se_log   = round(sapply(fits_F, se_logspr), 3),
           row.names = NULL)
#>      option sigmaF SPR_last se_log
#> 1 fixed_0.3  0.300    0.166  0.113
#> 2     prior  0.172    0.171  0.104
#> 3      F_re  0.135    0.174  0.099
#> 4     no_RW     NA    0.159  0.121

sigmaF_flicc() returns the fixed or estimated σF\sigma_F (NA without a random walk). The SPR trajectories with 95% intervals, and the apical F by year (report$Fap):

plot_spr(fits_F, ci = TRUE)


F_by_option <- FLQuants(fixed_0.3 = fits_F$fixed_0.3$report$Fap,
                        prior     = fits_F$prior$report$Fap,
                        F_re      = fits_F$F_re$report$Fap,
                        no_RW     = fits_F$no_RW$report$Fap)
ggplot(F_by_option, aes(year, data, colour = qname)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Apical F", colour = NULL) + theme_bw()

The estimated σF\sigma_F of the penalised and random-effects options is much smaller than 0.3, so their F trajectories are smoother; without a random walk F follows each year’s composition. To see what σF\sigma_F does, the next runs fix it at a range of values (sigmaF_values):

sigmaF_values <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 1)

fits_sigmaF <- Map(function(sF) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", sigmaF = sF), se = FALSE)
}, sigmaF_values)
names(fits_sigmaF) <- paste0("sigmaF_", sigmaF_values)

plot_spr(fits_sigmaF)

data.frame(sigmaF   = sigmaF_values,
           SPR_last = round(sapply(fits_sigmaF, sprcur_flicc), 3),
           neg_logL = round(sapply(fits_sigmaF, function(fit) fit$opt$objective), 1))
#>             sigmaF SPR_last neg_logL
#> sigmaF_0.05   0.05    0.160  36964.8
#> sigmaF_0.1    0.10    0.172  36966.7
#> sigmaF_0.3    0.30    0.166  36979.6
#> sigmaF_0.6    0.60    0.161  36991.6
#> sigmaF_1      1.00    0.160  37002.0

Small values force F (and SPR) towards a flat line; from about 0.3 upward the trajectories change little. The objective (neg_logL) includes the random-walk penalty, which is why it cannot be used to choose σF\sigma_F directly: it always favours the smallest value that the compositions tolerate.

13.1 Default: sigmaF fixed

sigmaF = 0.3 (the default) fixes the year-to-year standard deviation of log F, roughly a 30% typical annual change. It is fast, cannot collapse, and the simulations showed that it removes most of the smoothing lag (next section). Change it where fleet dynamics are known to be smoother (0.2) or more variable (0.5).

13.2 Estimating sigmaF with a prior (penalised)

With prior_sigmaF = c(mu, sd, 1), σF\sigma_F is a fixed-effect parameter and the objective is −logL=−logLdata−∑g,ylogϕ(logFg,y−logFg,y−1;0,σF)−logϕ(logσF;μ,sd). -\log L = -\log L_{data} - \sum_{g,y} \log \phi\left(\log F_{g,y} - \log F_{g,y-1};\, 0, \sigma_F\right) - \log \phi\left(\log \sigma_F;\, \mu, sd\right). Each random-walk term contributes −logσF-\log \sigma_F, so the joint maximum favours small σF\sigma_F with flat F whenever the data do not resist: the estimate is pulled down (here 0.172), and only the prior keeps it away from 0. Without a prior (prior_sigmaF = c(NA, NA, 1)) it collapses; FLicc warns.

13.3 F as random effects (F_re = TRUE)

The log F are integrated out, L(θ)=∫Ldata(θ,𝐅)p(𝐅∣σF)d𝐅, L(\theta) = \int L_{data}(\theta, \mathbf F)\, p(\mathbf F \mid \sigma_F)\, d\mathbf F, by the Laplace approximation (TMB): for each value of the other parameters θ\theta (selectivity, σF\sigma_F), the F path is optimised and the curvature around it enters the marginal likelihood. Consequences:

  • σF\sigma_F is estimated from the marginal likelihood, which properly accounts for the uncertainty of the F path (here 0.135). It can still go to small values when the compositions carry little year-to-year information; a weak prior c(log(0.3), 0.5, 1) is used unless another is given.
  • Standard errors (e.g. of log SPR) include the uncertainty of the F process.
  • Fitting is slower:
system.time(fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = f_settings$fixed_0.3))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    0.37    0.00    0.99
system.time(fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = f_settings$F_re))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    4.72    0.00    9.56

Use it for a final assessment and to estimate σF\sigma_F once; then fix it for repeated fits: sigmaF = sigmaF_flicc(fit_re). F_re = TRUE with sigmaF given keeps the random effects but fixes σF\sigma_F.

13.4 No random walk and separate years

prior_sigmaF = FALSE estimates each year’s F freely with shared selectivity (LBSPR fitted year by year, with common selectivity): no smoothing lag, but noisier F and no information for years without data. by_year = TRUE fits each year completely separately (including selectivity).

Option Settings sigmaF Use
fixed (default) sigmaF = 0.3 fixed routine, MSE, ensembles
penalised with prior prior_sigmaF = c(log(0.5), 0.3, 1) estimated, pulled down comparison with earlier versions
random effects F_re = TRUE marginal likelihood final assessment; estimate sigmaF once
no random walk prior_sigmaF = FALSE – complete data, maximum responsiveness
separate years by_year = TRUE – checks of selectivity change

13.5 Joint fit versus each year separately

by_year = TRUE fits every year on its own and re-estimates all parameters, including selectivity, for each year: the LBSPR-style approach. The comparison below uses the same data and settings as the reference fit fit.

fit_by_year <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                      settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"), by_year = TRUE)

plot_spr(list(joint = fit, by_year = fit_by_year))

plot_sel(flicc_stklen(fit_by_year))

The by-year selectivities differ between years although the gears did not change; these differences are sampling noise taken up by selectivity, and they pass on to F and SPR. The joint fit estimates one selectivity per gear and gives a smoother, more precise SPR series. Use by_year = TRUE as a check for real changes in selectivity (a new mesh size, a change of fishing grounds), not as the main assessment.

13.6 Lag under changing F

An equilibrium model explains each year’s composition by the equilibrium at that year’s F. After a change in F, the large fish adjust only over many years, so the estimated SPR lags behind (simulation, rebuild from 3x to 0.7x Fmsy):

F model SPR trend recovered, no cut with cut at 0.8 Linf
sigmaF estimated (collapsing) 14% 26%
sigmaF fixed 0.3 27% 50%
sigmaF fixed 1 29% 57%
no random walk 30% 59%

The smoothing lag of the random walk is largely removed at sigmaF = 0.3; larger values add little responsiveness but more year-to-year noise (+10 to +50%). The rest of the lag comes from the data (the tail carries the memory of past F) and from recruitment rising during recovery under a stock-recruitment relationship. In a rebuild from deep depletion the equilibrium model stays pessimistic.

14 Growth variability and life-history priors

14.1 CVL

CVL is the coefficient of variation of Linf among growth-type groups. It sets how far individual growth spreads the length composition, mostly in the tail: the fastest-growing groups determine how many fish occur near and beyond Linf. It is fixed at its input value unless CVL.sd is given; typical values are 0.07-0.15.

The sensitivity below refits the model for three CVL values (cvl_values), without and with a tail cut at 47 cm; Map() runs one fit per value.

cvl_values <- c(0.07, 0.10, 0.13)

fits_cvl <- Map(function(cvl) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = cvl, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"), se = FALSE)
}, cvl_values)
names(fits_cvl) <- paste0("CVL_", cvl_values)

fits_cvl_cut <- Map(function(cvl) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = cvl, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", tail_cut = 47), se = FALSE)
}, cvl_values)
names(fits_cvl_cut) <- paste0("CVL_", cvl_values, "_cut47")

cvl_table <- data.frame(CVL       = cvl_values,
                        SPR_no_cut = round(sapply(fits_cvl, sprcur_flicc), 3),
                        SPR_cut47  = round(sapply(fits_cvl_cut, sprcur_flicc), 3),
                        row.names = NULL)
cvl_table
#>    CVL SPR_no_cut SPR_cut47
#> 1 0.07      0.189     0.254
#> 2 0.10      0.166     0.247
#> 3 0.13      0.145     0.236
plot_spr(c(fits_cvl, fits_cvl_cut))

Status is sensitive to CVL because CVL shapes the tail: here SPR ranges 0.145-0.189 over CVL 0.07-0.13 without a cut and 0.236-0.254 with a cut at 47 cm.

14.2 maxsd and ngtg

The growth groups are placed at zhz_h on seq(-maxsd, maxsd, length = ngtg) with normal weights. Truncating the normal at maxsd reduces the realised CV of the groups below CVL and caps the largest group at L∞(1+maxsd⋅CVL)L_\infty(1 + \text{maxsd}\cdot\text{CVL}):

The realised spread can be computed directly from the group positions z and their normal weights w; the factor multiplies CVL:

z <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 13)          # maxsd = 2, ngtg = 13 (LBSPR)
w <- dnorm(z) / sum(dnorm(z))
sqrt(sum(w * z^2))                        # realised CV factor
#> [1] 0.9115967

z <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 13)          # maxsd = 3, ngtg = 13 (default)
w <- dnorm(z) / sum(dnorm(z))
sqrt(sum(w * z^2))
#> [1] 0.9938892

55.7 * (1 + c(2, 3) * 0.1)                # largest group Linf for maxsd 2 and 3
#> [1] 66.84 72.41

With the LBSPR default (maxsd = 2, 13 groups) the realised CV is about 0.9 x CVL; maxsd = 3 gives almost exactly CVL and allows larger fish. The number of groups matters little beyond about 13, and computing time grows with it.

The fits below compare LBSPR’s grid with the default and a finer grid (maxsd_values with matching ngtg_values), without and with the tail cut; Map() takes the two vectors in parallel.

maxsd_values <- c(2, 3, 3)
ngtg_values  <- c(13, 13, 19)

fits_maxsd <- Map(function(maxsd, ngtg) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", maxsd = maxsd, ngtg = ngtg), se = FALSE)
}, maxsd_values, ngtg_values)

fits_maxsd_cut <- Map(function(maxsd, ngtg) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", maxsd = maxsd, ngtg = ngtg,
                         tail_cut = 47), se = FALSE)
}, maxsd_values, ngtg_values)

data.frame(maxsd      = maxsd_values,
           ngtg       = ngtg_values,
           SPR_no_cut = round(sapply(fits_maxsd, sprcur_flicc), 3),
           SPR_cut47  = round(sapply(fits_maxsd_cut, sprcur_flicc), 3))
#>   maxsd ngtg SPR_no_cut SPR_cut47
#> 1     2   13      0.172     0.250
#> 2     3   13      0.166     0.247
#> 3     3   19      0.166     0.247

The default is maxsd = 3, ngtg = 13 (from FLicc 1.0.11; before: LBSPR’s maxsd = 2, ngtg = 13); 19 groups give the same result at about 25% more computing time. With maxsd = 2 the largest group is 1.2L∞1.2 L_\infty at CVL = 0.1, and fish above it get a near-zero probability: each such fish costs about the same in the likelihood. In sensitivity runs and Monte Carlo draws with a lower Linf or CVL, this gives steps in the AIC and failed refits. maxsd = 3 extends the groups to 1.3L∞1.3 L_\infty, and CVL is then close to the realised spread, which matters when CVL is taken from external growth studies (with maxsd = 2, a CVL input of 0.1 corresponds to a realised spread of about 0.09). At the input life history the two settings usually give similar results. Use maxsd = 2 to reproduce LBSPR.

14.3 Estimating Linf, M/k and CVL with priors

By default growth and natural mortality are fixed. linf.sd, Mk.sd and CVL.sd estimate them with normal priors on the log scale around the inputs: logL∞∼N(logL∞in,𝚕𝚒𝚗𝚏.𝚜𝚍2),log(M/k)∼N(log(M/k)in,𝙼𝚔.𝚜𝚍2),logCVL∼N(logCVLin,𝙲𝚅𝙻.𝚜𝚍2), \log L_\infty \sim N(\log L_\infty^{in}, \texttt{linf.sd}^2), \quad \log (M/k) \sim N(\log (M/k)^{in}, \texttt{Mk.sd}^2), \quad \log \mathrm{CVL} \sim N(\log \mathrm{CVL}^{in}, \texttt{CVL.sd}^2), so each sd is approximately a CV (e.g. linf.sd = 0.05: about ±10% at 95%).

The fit below estimates all three with priors. The estimates are on the log scale: L∞L_\infty = exp(log_Linf), M/kM/k = exp(log_Mk) and CVL = 1 / sqrt(exp(log_Galpha)); the column se is approximately the posterior CV (for log_Galpha divide by 2).

fit_pri <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                  settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating",
                                  linf.sd = 0.05, Mk.sd = 0.1, CVL.sd = 0.25))

est <- fit_pri$par[fit_pri$par$par %in% c("log_Linf", "log_Mk", "log_Galpha"), ]
est
#>          par       mpd         se
#> 1   log_Linf 3.8968682 0.04119969
#> 2 log_Galpha 4.7193829 0.35243888
#> 3     log_Mk 0.6893467 0.10633810
exp(est$mpd[est$par == "log_Linf"])            # Linf (input 55.7)
#> [1] 49.24797
exp(est$mpd[est$par == "log_Mk"])              # M/k  (input 0.162 / 0.08 = 2.03)
#> [1] 1.992413
1 / sqrt(exp(est$mpd[est$par == "log_Galpha"])) # CVL  (input 0.1)
#> [1] 0.09444936

plot_spr(list(fixed = fit, priors = fit_pri), ci = TRUE)

Here the length data pull Linf up to about 49.2 (posterior CV 0.041 against a prior CV of 0.05), and because a larger Linf means the fish in the catch are relatively younger, SPR drops markedly. The posterior CVs of M/k and CVL stay close to their prior CVs: the data say little about them. A shift of this size in Linf is a finding to check against growth studies, not a result to accept; run the assessment with Linf fixed at the alternative values as a sensitivity.

Notes:

  • k is not estimated separately: the length model depends on M/k (and Z/k), so uncertainty in k and M is expressed through Mk.sd. k still sets the time scale of the annual F estimates (F is estimated as F/k).
  • Length data carry limited information on Linf and CVL, and both are confounded with dome-shaped selectivity and the tail; a posterior CV close to the prior CV means the data are uninformative. Large moves away from the input (several prior SDs) indicate a conflict between the data and the life history, to be investigated rather than accepted.
  • For ensembles, drawing the life-history parameters and keeping them fixed in each fit (mc_flicc()) is usually better behaved than estimating them.

15 Tail of the length composition

15.1 Tail cut

tail_cut = L excludes bins with lower bound ≥L\geq L from the likelihood; observed and predicted compositions are truncated and the predictions renormalised, πl∣L<Lcut=πl/∑l′:Ll′<Lcutπl′. \pi_{l \mid L < L_{cut}} = \pi_l \Big/ \sum_{l' : L_{l'} < L_{cut}} \pi_{l'} . This is exact conditioning: the model still describes the whole population with its input CVL, SPR and reference points use all lengths, and CVL needs no adjustment. tail_cut is an absolute length (as Lplus), so all sensitivity runs and ensemble draws use the same bins. (Values <= 1.5 are read as a fraction of Linf, with a warning.)

fit_cut <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                  settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", tail_cut = 47))  # ~0.85 x Linf
fit_cut$tmb_data$LLB[fit_cut$tmb_data$cut_bin + 1]
#> [1] 47
plot_spr(list(no_cut = fit, cut_47 = fit_cut), ci = TRUE)

Simulation (stable F, correct Linf unless stated):

no cut cut at 0.80-0.85 x Linf
CVL input 0.07 / 0.10 / 0.13 (true 0.1) +9 / -1 / -11% +13 / +9 / +4%
strong dome on one gear fitted as logistic -17% +1%
SPR trend recovered in a rebuild (sigmaF 0.3) 27% ~50%
Linf input 0.9 / 1.1 x true +91 / -40% +74 / -28%

The cut halves the CVL sensitivity, removes the bias of a strong unmodelled dome and roughly doubles responsiveness; it costs a small positive bias (+7 to +10%) and more noise under stable F, and does not remove the Linf sensitivity. Starting value: 0.80-0.85 x Linf, fixed across fits.

15.2 Plus group, robust likelihood, GTG range

  • Lplus = L pools bins with lower bound ≥L\geq L into one (the total counts, the shape does not).
  • rob_eps = 0.001 bounds the cost of a few fish in bins the model barely reaches.
  • The largest growth group stops at L∞(1+maxsd⋅CVL)L_\infty(1 + \text{maxsd}\cdot\text{CVL}) (1.3 Linf with the default maxsd = 3 and CVL = 0.1). Fish beyond it get near-zero probability, and fiticc() warns about them (tail_warning, default TRUE); a tail cut makes this irrelevant.

16 Model equations and comparison of models

16.1 Fishing mortality and total mortality

Fg,y(L)=Fg,ySg(L)F_{g,y}(L) = F_{g,y} S_g(L), Zy(L)=M(L)+∑gFg,y(L)Z_y(L) = M(L) + \sum_g F_{g,y}(L). Gear shares of F are informed by catch_by_gear through a soft constraint on the predicted catch shares (catch.sd, default 0.05), in weight by default: logĈg,ywĈG,yw∼N(logcg,ycG,y,𝚌𝚊𝚝𝚌𝚑.𝚜𝚍2),Ĉg,yw=∑LCg,y(L)W(L), \log\frac{\hat C^w_{g,y}}{\hat C^w_{G,y}} \sim N\!\left(\log\frac{c_{g,y}}{c_{G,y}},\ \texttt{catch.sd}^2\right), \qquad \hat C^w_{g,y} = \sum_L C_{g,y}(L)\, W(L), where cg,yc_{g,y} is catch_by_gear and GG the last gear. The predicted shares are in fit$report$catch_share. With settings$catch_units = "numbers" the shares are compared in numbers, Ĉg,y=∑LCg,y(L)\hat C_{g,y} = \sum_L C_{g,y}(L), as in fishblicc (Medley 2025); use this when the catch split is known in numbers.

16.2 Expected catch and length composition

FLicc separates the population model (expected numbers at length under growth, M, F and selectivity) from the observation model (the likelihood that links the observed counts to the expected composition), so either can be changed without the other. With NiN_i the expected number of fish entering length bin ii, the expected catch of gear gg in bin ii is Ci,g=Fi,gZi(Ni−Ni+1),Zi=Mi+∑gFi,g, C_{i,g} = \frac{F_{i,g}}{Z_i}\left(N_i - N_{i+1}\right), \qquad Z_i = M_i + \sum_g F_{i,g}, and the expected composition of gear gg is πi,g=Ci,g/∑iCi,g\pi_{i,g} = C_{i,g} / \sum_i C_{i,g}.

16.3 Population model

pop_model = "gtg" (default, as LBSPR): growth-type groups L∞,h=L∞(1+CVLzh)L_{\infty,h} = L_\infty(1 + \mathrm{CVL}\, z_h), zhz_h on seq(-maxsd, maxsd, length = ngtg) (13 groups, maxsd = 2), weights ωh∝ϕ(zh)\omega_h \propto \phi(z_h). Within a group, survival across bin ii follows from the time needed to grow through it under von Bertalanffy growth: Ni+1,h=Ni,h(L∞,h−Li+1L∞,h−Li)Zi/k,Ni=∑hωhNi,h. N_{i+1,h} = N_{i,h}\left(\frac{L_{\infty,h} - L_{i+1}}{L_{\infty,h} - L_i}\right)^{Z_i/k}, \qquad N_i = \sum_h \omega_h N_{i,h}.

pop_model = "gamma" follows fishblicc: Linf is gamma-distributed among individuals, and the numbers at length integrate survival over that distribution, Ni=∫f(L∞)Si(L∞)dL∞, N_i = \int f(L_\infty)\, S_i(L_\infty)\, dL_\infty , evaluated by Gauss-Laguerre quadrature (slower). Both are equilibrium models: each year is explained by the equilibrium at that year’s F (section Lag under changing F on the consequences).

16.4 Observation model

For gear gg in year yy, with counts 𝐲g,y\mathbf y_{g,y} and total ng,yn_{g,y}:

  • obs_model = "mn" (default): 𝐲g,y∼Multinomial(ng,y,𝛑g,y)\mathbf y_{g,y} \sim \text{Multinomial}(n_{g,y}, \boldsymbol\pi_{g,y}).
  • "nb": yi,g,y∼NB(μ,ϕ)y_{i,g,y} \sim \text{NB}(\mu, \phi) with μ=ng,yπi,g,y\mu = n_{g,y}\pi_{i,g,y} and Var=μ+μ2/ϕ\text{Var} = \mu + \mu^2/\phi; ϕ\phi is estimated.
  • "dm": 𝐲g,y∼Dirichlet-multinomial(ng,y,α0𝛑g,y)\mathbf y_{g,y} \sim \text{Dirichlet-multinomial}(n_{g,y}, \alpha_0 \boldsymbol\pi_{g,y}) with α0=ng,y\alpha_0 = n_{g,y} (dm_theta = "fixed") or estimated ("linear", "saturating").

How the sample size enters each of them is explained in section Effective sample size and observation models; the models are compared on the same data below.

16.5 Comparison of models

The population model (gtg or gamma) and the observation model (mn, dm, nb) can be combined freely. The four fits below differ only in these two settings; Map() runs one fit per list of settings.

model_settings <- list(
  gtg_mn   = list(CVL = 0.1, pop_model = "gtg",   obs_model = "mn"),
  gtg_dm   = list(CVL = 0.1, pop_model = "gtg",   obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"),
  gtg_nb   = list(CVL = 0.1, pop_model = "gtg",   obs_model = "nb"),
  gamma_nb = list(CVL = 0.1, pop_model = "gamma", obs_model = "nb"))   # as fishblicc

fits_model <- Map(function(set) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg, settings = set)
}, model_settings)

data.frame(model    = names(fits_model),
           SPR_last = round(sapply(fits_model, sprcur_flicc), 3),
           se_log   = round(sapply(fits_model, se_logspr), 3),
           row.names = NULL)
#>      model SPR_last se_log
#> 1   gtg_mn    0.174  0.095
#> 2   gtg_dm    0.166  0.113
#> 3   gtg_nb    0.157  0.105
#> 4 gamma_nb    0.156  0.105
plot_spr(fits_model, ci = TRUE)

The gamma model integrates over Linf numerically and is slower:

system.time(fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                   settings = model_settings$gtg_nb))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    0.40    0.00    0.89
system.time(fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                   settings = model_settings$gamma_nb))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    3.40    0.64    7.74

Log-likelihoods and AIC are not comparable between observation models (they are likelihoods of different things); compare the estimates, their precision and the fit to the compositions (plot_len). Differences between gtg and gamma show the sensitivity to the approximation of growth variability, differences between mn, dm and nb the weight and robustness given to the compositions.

Purpose pop_model obs_model Comment
Routine assessment, MSE "gtg" "dm" fast; robust with real data
LBSPR-style "gtg" "mn" fastest; sensitive to the ESS; LBSPR fits each year separately (by_year = TRUE) with Linf, M/k and CVL fixed
LBB "gtg", ngtg = 1 "dm", fixed precision lbb_flicc(); Reproducing LBB
fishblicc replication "gamma" "nb" slower; closest to fishblicc

17 Reproducing LBSPR, LBB and fishblicc

Each of the three tools is a configuration of FLicc (table in section FLicc: a framework for length-interval catch curves). This section fits each tool’s configuration to the tool’s own example data, compares the results with the tool’s published output, and adds FLicc’s default for comparison.

17.1 LBSPR: the multi-year example

LBSPR (Hordyk et al. 2015, 2016) fits the GTG model (13 growth-type groups, CV of Linf 0.1, groups over ±2\pm 2 SD; FLicc’s default since 1.0.11 is 13 groups over ±3\pm 3 SD, so LBSPR’s grid is set explicitly with ngtg = 13, maxsd = 2) with a multinomial likelihood to each year separately, with Linf, M/k and CVL fixed, and estimates SL50, SL95 and F/M (apical F over M) by year. The example is LBSPR’s multi-year length-frequency file LFreq_MultiYrHead.csv (six years, 5-mm classes) with the life history of LBSPR’s vignette: Linf = 100 mm, M/k = 1.5, L50 = 66 mm, L95 = 70 mm. It is included in FLicc as data("lbspr_test"), with LBSPR’s estimates for these data:

data("lbspr_test")   # lfd_lbspr, lhpar_lbspr, lbspr_est
lfd_lbspr

Three fits: LBSPR’s configuration (multinomial, LBSPR’s growth-type groups, each year separately), the same likelihood and groups with all years fitted jointly (one selectivity, random walk on F), and FLicc’s default (Dirichlet-multinomial with estimated precision, maxsd = 3, years jointly). For the separate years Map() fits one model per year:

set_lbspr <- list(CVL = 0.1, ngtg = 13, maxsd = 2, obs_model = "mn")
yrs_lbspr <- dimnames(stk_lbspr)$year
fits_lbspr_y <- Map(function(y) {
  lfd_y <- FLQuants(lapply(lfd_lbspr, function(x) x[, y]))
  fiticc(lfd_y, stocklen(lfd_y, lhpar_lbspr, m_model = "constant"), sel_fun = "logistic",
         catch_by_gear = 1, settings = set_lbspr, verbose = FALSE)
}, yrs_lbspr)
fit_lbspr_j <- fiticc(lfd_lbspr, stk_lbspr, sel_fun = "logistic", catch_by_gear = 1,
                      settings = set_lbspr)
fit_lbspr_d <- fiticc(lfd_lbspr, stk_lbspr, sel_fun = "logistic", catch_by_gear = 1,
                      settings = list(CVL = 0.1))

LBSPR’s results for these data (LBSPRfit()) are in lbspr_est: the yearly point estimates, and the estimates smoothed over the years with a Kalman filter (@Ests, LBSPR’s default output). The FLicc estimates are taken from the fits (selectivity from the parameters, F/M as apical F over M, SPR):

lbspr_out <- lbspr_est[, c("year", "SL50", "SL95", "FM", "SPR")]
lbspr_smooth <- setNames(lbspr_est[, c("year", "SL50_smooth", "SL95_smooth", "FM_smooth", "SPR_smooth")],
                         c("year", "SL50", "SL95", "FM", "SPR"))
est_flicc <- function(f) {
  sm <- exp(f$obj$env$parList(par = f$obj$env$last.par.best)$Sm) * 100   # relative to Linf
  data.frame(year = as.numeric(f$tmb_data$year_names), SL50 = sm[1], SL95 = sm[1] + sm[2],
             FM = as.numeric(f$report$Fap) / 0.3, SPR = as.numeric(f$report$spr))
}
lbspr_runs <- list("LBSPR, by year" = lbspr_out,
                   "LBSPR, smoothed" = lbspr_smooth,
                   "FLicc mn, by year" = do.call(rbind, lapply(fits_lbspr_y, est_flicc)),
                   "FLicc mn, joint" = est_flicc(fit_lbspr_j),
                   "FLicc default" = est_flicc(fit_lbspr_d))
lbspr_tab <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(x, nm) cbind(run = nm, round(x, 3)), lbspr_runs, names(lbspr_runs)))
rownames(lbspr_tab) <- NULL
lbspr_tab

lbspr_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("SL50", "FM", "SPR"), function(v)
  data.frame(lbspr_tab[, c("run", "year")], what = v, value = lbspr_tab[[v]])))
lbspr_long$run <- factor(lbspr_long$run, levels = names(lbspr_runs))
ggplot(lbspr_long, aes(year, value, colour = run)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~what, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "grey55", "#E69F00", "#0072B2", "#009E73")) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL, colour = NULL) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

plot_spr(fit_lbspr_d, ci = TRUE)

With LBSPR’s configuration (obs_model = "mn", ngtg = 13, maxsd = 2, each year separately) FLicc reproduces LBSPR’s yearly estimates: SPR differs from LBSPR’s by 0.032 on average, F/M by 0.006. The yearly estimates vary (here SPR from 0.3507105 to 0.5404657 and SL50 from 46.35 to 50.05), and LBSPR smooths them afterwards with a Kalman filter. FLicc’s joint fit links the years inside the model instead: one selectivity for all years and a random walk on F, so the data of all years inform each year’s F through the likelihood rather than by smoothing the point estimates afterwards; the figure compares it with LBSPR’s smoothed series.

At the same SL50, SL95 and F/M, FLicc’s SPR is about 0.03 lower than LBSPR’s in every year. The difference is in the spawning output per recruit, not in the fit, and has two sources in LBSPR’s GTG model (LBSPRsim_()):

  1. Selectivity in the survival recursion. LBSPR computes the selectivity that enters survival as 1/(1 + exp(-log(19) * (LBins - (SL50 + By/2)) / (SL95 - SL50))) at the class lower bounds LBins (By = class width), i.e. at one class below the class midpoint, while the predicted catch uses selectivity at the midpoints. Fish are therefore fished as if they were one class (here 5 mm) smaller, which lowers F at length in the survival and raises SPR. The fit, and so SL50 and F/M, is driven by the catch and is not affected.

    Note — possible error in LBSPR (LBSPRsim_.r, LBSPR 0.1.9): line 168 evaluates survival selectivity at LBins - (SL50 + 0.5*By), a full class below the midpoint; the M/K line next to it (line 171) uses the midpoint LBins + 0.5*By, and the predicted catch (line 218) uses selectivity at the midpoints LMids. The model thus applies two selectivity curves one class apart, one to the catch and one to the mortality. The intended expression was probably (LBins + 0.5*By) - SL50. As a consequence LBSPR’s SPR is biased upwards by an amount that grows with the class width: for the 2010 estimates (SL50 = 49.1, SL95 = 62.9, F/M = 0.56) LBSPR’s equations give SPR = 0.406, 0.413, 0.437 and 0.483 for 1, 2, 5 and 10-mm classes, against 0.399–0.404 with selectivity at the midpoints. SL50, SL95 and F/M are not affected. LBSPR’s pseudo-age model (Control = list(modtype = "absel")) uses midpoints throughout.

  2. Maturity at the same relative size. LBSPR scales the maturity ogive with each group’s Linf (L50,g=L50L∞,g/L∞L_{50,g} = L_{50}\,L_{\infty,g}/L_\infty), whereas FLicc uses one maturity-at-length ogive for all groups. Here this changes SPR by only about 0.005, in the opposite direction.

Neither enters the likelihood, so spr_gtg_flicc() can recompute the SPR of a GTG fit afterwards: mat = "relative" uses LBSPR’s maturity at relative size, and sel_lag = 1 applies F at length one class late, as in LBSPR’s survival recursion. Both inputs are fixed, so the ratio adj = spr_gtg / spr is a correction factor: it scales FLicc’s SPR and its interval and leaves the uncertainty (the SE of log SPR) as it is. With mat = "length" and sel_lag = 0 it returns FLicc’s own SPR (adj = 1):

spr_y <- function(f) {
  data.frame(year = as.numeric(f$tmb_data$year_names),
             FLicc = spr_gtg_flicc(f, mat = "length")$spr,
             mat_rel = spr_gtg_flicc(f)$spr_gtg,
             mat_rel_lag = spr_gtg_flicc(f, sel_lag = 1)$spr_gtg)
}
spr_cmp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits_lbspr_y, spr_y))
cbind(round(spr_cmp, 3), LBSPR = round(lbspr_out$SPR, 3))
#>      year FLicc mat_rel mat_rel_lag LBSPR
#> 2010 2010 0.404   0.399       0.436 0.437
#> 2011 2011 0.406   0.401       0.438 0.439
#> 2012 2012 0.400   0.395       0.431 0.432
#> 2013 2013 0.450   0.446       0.481 0.483
#> 2014 2014 0.315   0.310       0.350 0.351
#> 2015 2015 0.513   0.509       0.538 0.540
spr_gtg_flicc(fit_lbspr_d, sel_lag = 1)   # joint default fit, LBSPR-type SPR with interval
#>   year       spr   spr_gtg      adj       lwr       upr
#> 1 2010 0.3915624 0.4227786 1.079722 0.3231389 0.5531422
#> 2 2011 0.3881664 0.4194598 1.080618 0.3250818 0.5412377
#> 3 2012 0.3875531 0.4188602 1.080781 0.3265716 0.5372294
#> 4 2013 0.4122634 0.4429717 1.074487 0.3496501 0.5612008
#> 5 2014 0.3387641 0.3709648 1.095053 0.2825345 0.4870728
#> 6 2015 0.3870813 0.4183989 1.080907 0.3183125 0.5499553

With both LBSPR conventions the yearly FLicc SPR differs from LBSPR’s by 0.001 on average, against 0.032 for FLicc’s own SPR. FLicc keeps its own SPR as the default, because it applies the fitted selectivity consistently to the catch and the survival. The default growth-type groups (maxsd = 3) also differ from LBSPR’s: they reach 1.3 instead of 1.2 Linf, so a few large fish no longer get a near-zero probability, and CVL is the realised spread of Linf rather than about 0.9 of it (section maxsd and ngtg). The default likelihood estimates how much weight the compositions carry and widens the intervals accordingly.

17.2 LBB: the Illex example

17.2.1 LBB as a special case of the GTG model

LBB (Froese et al. 2018) describes the numbers surviving to length class jj (lower bound LjL_j) with one growth type, Nj=Nj−1(L∞−LjL∞−Lj−1)M/K+(F/K)Sj, N_j = N_{j-1}\left(\frac{L_\infty - L_j}{L_\infty - L_{j-1}}\right)^{M/K + (F/K)\,S_j}, where SjS_j is a logistic selectivity with length at 50% selection LcL_c and slope α\alpha (relative to L∞L_\infty). This is FLicc’s GTG recursion with a single growth-type group (pop_model = "gtg", ngtg = 1). Each year is fitted separately, with a prior on Linf (CV at most 1%, from an nls() fit to the aggregated frequencies, or a user value), on M/K (1.5, SD 0.15) and, in LBB, also on LcL_c and α\alpha; the likelihood is a Dirichlet on the relative frequencies with a concentration of 10410^4.

The expected catch in a length class can be computed in two ways:

  • with the pile-up correction (Hordyk et al. 2019; FLicc’s model and LBB with Pile = 1): the numbers in the class are the survivors integrated over the time spent in it, Cj∝Sj(Nj−Nj+1)/(M/K+(F/K)Sj)C_j \propto S_j\,(N_j - N_{j+1})/(M/K + (F/K) S_j). Fish grow more slowly towards Linf, so they accumulate in the large classes;
  • without it (LBB Pile = 0, the setting of LBB’s example stocks): the catch is proportional to the survivorship at the class bound, Cj∝SjNjC_j \propto S_j N_j.

lbb_flicc() sets FLicc up as LBB: one growth type, one gear (gears pooled), Linf and M/K priors from lbb_priors_flicc() (LBB’s guess step) or user values, lengths at or above the Linf prior excluded, and each year fitted separately (by_year = TRUE) or jointly with a random walk on F (by_year = FALSE). The options pile (LBB’s Pile) and ess (data weighting; ess = 20000 with a fixed Dirichlet-multinomial precision corresponds to LBB’s concentration of 10410^4) allow LBB’s settings to be matched. Selectivity is estimated without priors. lbbref_flicc() gives LBB’s quantities by year (Linf, Lc, M/K, F/K, F/M, Z/K, Lopt, Lc_opt, B/B0 from LBB’s Beverton-Holt equations) next to FLicc’s EPR and SPR, and plot_lbb() LBB’s summary figure.

17.2.2 The Illex fit

The example uses LBB’s own example stock Illex coindetii (Adriatic) with the settings of LBB’s Example_ID.csv: the years 1996, 1999, 2001, 2002, 2009, 2014 and 2016, Linf set to 23 cm, Lm50 16 cm and Pile = 0. The data are read from the LBB repository (lengths in mm, converted to cm) and raised to 1000 per year:

url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SISTA16/LBB/master/Example_Dat.csv"
lbb_dat <- tryCatch(read.csv(url), error = function(e) NULL)
have_lbb <- !is.null(lbb_dat)
if (have_lbb) {
  d <- subset(lbb_dat, Stock == "Ille_coi_AD" & !is.na(CatchNo))
  d <- aggregate(CatchNo ~ Year + Length, data = d, FUN = sum)
  d$data <- d$CatchNo / ave(d$CatchNo, d$Year, FUN = sum) * 1000
  lfd_illex <- FLQuantLen(lfd_long_to_wide(data.frame(len = d$Length / 10, year = d$Year,
                                                      data = d$data, qname = "Illex")),
                          unit = "cm", midL = FALSE)
}
yrs_illex <- c(1996, 1999, 2001, 2002, 2009, 2014, 2016)

Three fits: LBB’s settings (pile = 0, LBB’s data weighting), the same with the pile-up correction, and FLicc’s joint fit of all years with the pile-up correction and the estimated Dirichlet-multinomial precision:

fit_lbb0 <- lbb_flicc(lfd_illex, Linf = 23, Lm50 = 16, years = yrs_illex,
                      pile = 0, ess = 20000)
fit_lbb1 <- lbb_flicc(lfd_illex, Linf = 23, Lm50 = 16, years = yrs_illex,
                      pile = 1, ess = 20000)
fit_lbbj <- lbb_flicc(lfd_illex, Linf = 23, Lm50 = 16, years = yrs_illex,
                      by_year = FALSE)
fit_lbb0

LBB’s own results for this stock (LBB_33a.R, MCMC medians) are entered as a table and compared by year:

lbb_out <- data.frame(year = yrs_illex,
                      ZK  = c(2.32, 3.12, 2.57, 3.72, 3.15, 5.24, 6.85),
                      FM  = c(0.265, 0.878, 0.732, 1.467, 0.910, 2.713, 3.570),
                      BB0 = c(0.699, 0.267, 0.293, 0.138, 0.294, 0.065, 0.044))
runs <- list("LBB (JAGS)" = lbb_out, "FLicc, Pile = 0" = fit_lbb0$table,
             "FLicc, Pile = 1" = fit_lbb1$table, "FLicc, Pile = 1, joint" = fit_lbbj$table)
cmp <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(x, nm) data.frame(run = nm, year = x$year, ZK = x$ZK,
                                                     FM = x$FM, BB0 = x$BB0), runs, names(runs)))
cmp$run <- factor(cmp$run, levels = names(runs))
long <- rbind(data.frame(cmp[, 1:2], what = "Z/K", value = cmp$ZK),
              data.frame(cmp[, 1:2], what = "F/M", value = cmp$FM),
              data.frame(cmp[, 1:2], what = "B/B0", value = cmp$BB0))
ggplot(long, aes(year, value, colour = run)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~what, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "#E69F00", "#0072B2", "#009E73")) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

dif <- function(x) round(mean(x$ZK - lbb_out$ZK), 2)

The same comparison with plot_epr() and plot_spr(): LBB’s B/B0 next to FLicc’s exploitable potential ratio (EPR, the same quantity from the FLicc engine), with LBB’s reference points (B/B0 at F = M and Lc = Lc_opt, a proxy for Bmsy/B0, and half of it), and FLicc’s SPR, which LBB does not report:

yr_flq <- function(tab, col) FLQuant(matrix(tab[[col]], nrow = 1), dimnames = list(year = tab$year))
bfm <- attr(fit_lbb1$table, "BFM1B0")
plot_epr(FLQuants("LBB (JAGS)" = yr_flq(lbb_out, "BB0"),
                  "FLicc, Pile = 0" = yr_flq(fit_lbb0$table, "EPR"),
                  "FLicc, Pile = 1" = yr_flq(fit_lbb1$table, "EPR"),
                  "FLicc, Pile = 1, joint" = yr_flq(fit_lbbj$table, "EPR")),
         ref_levels = c(bfm, bfm / 2), title = "B/B0 (LBB) and EPR (FLicc)")

plot_spr(FLQuants("FLicc, Pile = 0" = yr_flq(fit_lbb0$table, "SPR"),
                  "FLicc, Pile = 1" = yr_flq(fit_lbb1$table, "SPR"),
                  "FLicc, Pile = 1, joint" = yr_flq(fit_lbbj$table, "SPR")))

With LBB’s settings (pile = 0) FLicc reproduces LBB: Z/K differs from LBB’s by -0.03 on average over the years, and F/M and B/B0 follow LBB’s estimates year by year. The remaining differences are small: LBB’s priors on α\alpha and F/K shape how Z/K is split into M/K and F/K (LBB’s M/K moves between 1.4 and 1.8 across years, FLicc’s stays near the prior of 1.5), and MCMC medians differ slightly from maximum likelihood estimates.

With the pile-up correction, Z/K is higher by 0.88 on average, so F/M is higher and B/B0 lower. Survivorship declines as about (L∞−L)Z/K(L_\infty - L)^{Z/K}, while the numbers in a class decline as about (L∞−L)Z/K−1(L_\infty - L)^{Z/K - 1}, so the model without the correction needs a Z/K about one unit lower to describe the same frequencies. The joint fit of all years (by_year = FALSE) shares selectivity and links F between years, which smooths the year-to-year changes in the separate fits.

plot_lbb(fit_lbb1)

17.2.3 Points to consider with LBB

  • Pile-up correction. Hordyk et al. (2019) pointed out that the numbers in a length class are the survivors integrated over the class, and that without the correction F is underestimated. Froese et al. (2019) argued that the correction matters most for continuous recruitment and sampling, and added it as an option to LBB. In LBB’s B/B0, computed from the Beverton-Holt equations, the integration is included; with Pile = 0 Z/K is therefore estimated with a different model from the one used for B/B0. FLicc uses the integrated numbers for estimation and status (pile = 1, default); pile = 0 is available to reproduce LBB.
  • Priors. LBB’s priors on LcL_c and in particular on α\alpha (SD 2.5%, centred on a value derived from each year’s ascending limb) fix much of the selectivity shape; together with the M/K prior they determine the split of Z/K into M/K and F/K, which the data alone barely inform. In FLicc these constraints are optional settings (priors, sel_fixed).
  • Separate years. Fitting each year separately lets selectivity and Linf change between years, which absorbs recruitment pulses as apparent changes in selectivity. The joint fit (by_year = FALSE) estimates one selectivity and links F between years.
  • Weighting. LBB’s Dirichlet concentration of 10410^4 gives the data a weight close to 10410^4 fish per year whatever the sample size; FLicc’s default estimates the precision from the data.

Within these choices, LBB’s estimates can be reproduced in FLicc, and each assumption can be switched separately to see its effect.

17.3 fishblicc: the Bombay duck example

FLicc includes the Bombay duck example of fishblicc (three gears) to check consistency with fishblicc. Natural mortality decreases with length (m_model = "inverse", M(L)=MLref/LM(L) = M\, L_{ref} / L with Lref=21.9L_{ref} = 21.9), and Linf, M/k and CVL are estimated with priors as in fishblicc. fishblicc compares the relative catch of each gear in numbers of fish (Medley 2025), so the catch shares are given in numbers here (catch_units = "numbers"):

data("fishblicc_example")
lhpar_fishblicc <- rbind(lhpar_fishblicc,
                         FLPar(M = lhpar_fishblicc["k"] * lhpar_fishblicc["Mk"]))
stklen_fishblicc <- stocklen(lfd_fishblicc, lhpar_fishblicc,
                             m_model = "inverse", reflen = 21.9)
fit_fishblicc <- fiticc(lfd_fishblicc, stklen_fishblicc,
                        sel_fun = c("dsnormal", "dsnormal", "dsnormal"),
                        catch_by_gear = c(0.1802070, 0.2101353, 0.6096577),
                        settings = list(pop_model = "gamma", obs_model = "nb",
                                        CVL = 0.14, CVL.sd = 0.1,
                                        linf.sd = 2 / 40, Mk.sd = 0.1,
                                        catch_units = "numbers"))
flicc_convergence(fit_fishblicc)

Part III: Management

18 Use in an MSE

flicc.sa() wraps fiticc() as the estimation step of an mse management procedure, with lbi.hcr(), rfb.flicc.hcr() and flicc.is() for the harvest control rule and implementation:

est <- mseCtrl(method = flicc.sa, args = list(
  lhpar = lhpar, sel_fun = sel_fun, ess.g = NULL,   # raw counts
  settings = list(obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", CVL = 0.1,
                  sigmaF = 0.3,      # fixed (or the F_re estimate from the real data)
                  tail_cut = 47,     # absolute length, the same in every iteration
                  spr_ref = 40),
  spr = 40))
  • se = FALSE is used inside flicc.sa(); fixed sigmaF avoids its estimation in every year and iteration.
  • The tail cut and sigmaF both trade responsiveness against stability; tune them together with the smoothing of the harvest control rule.
  • Expect the equilibrium model to be pessimistic during a rebuild and optimistic while F increases.

19 Summary of checks and recommendations

# Check Red flag Action
1 sample size by gear-year (plot_lfdn) < 50 fish or < 10 bins; gear mix changing ESS per gear; drop/pool poor gear-years
2 composition consistency (plot_lfd) shifts in mode or left limb split gears/periods; restrict years
3 largest fish vs Linf > 1% at or above Linf revisit Linf; tail cut
4 empirical catch curves (plot_zlcc) curved limbs, jumping slopes dome or tail cut; keep random walk
5 life-history inputs Linf inconsistent with data; odd M/k Linf sensitivity; priors (linf.sd) as a check
6 selectivity plausibility (plot_sel) narrow or unsupported domes logistic; fix from external data; dome sensitivity (dome_sens_flicc)
7 convergence (flicc_convergence) gradient, Hessian, bounds restarts; simplify; tail cut
8 fit to compositions (plot_len, plot_resid_bubble, lmean_resid_flicc, ppc_flicc) systematic misfit; failed runs test; many values outside predictive intervals selectivity, Linf, tail cut; lower ESS; cohort patterns are expected
9 retrospective rho beyond ±0.2 trends in selectivity or sampling
10 indicators vs status gears disagree best gear; pooling; HCR smoothing
Topic Recommendation
Observation model dm with real data
Sample size dm with dm_theta = "saturating" on raw counts or ESS >= 500 (the data set their weight); with fixed precision or mn, ESS about 150-200 per gear-year, never raw thousands
Growth fix Linf and CVL; Linf is the main sensitivity; default maxsd = 3, ngtg = 13 (maxsd = 2 only to reproduce LBSPR)
Selectivity logistic unless supported; always run dome_sens_flicc() (rsd 1000 to 0.4 x Linf); binormal/bidsnormal for two size modes
Sensitivity runs fits_summary() for the table; ensemble_flicc() with equal weights (AIC weights as a check, same data only)
Management options plot_contour_flicc(): yield and SPR (or SSB with s) over selectivity and F by gear
F over time random walk, sigmaF fixed (0.3 or the F_re estimate); by_year = TRUE only as a check
Tail tail_cut at about 0.80-0.85 x Linf, as a length
Missing data keep zeros, rely on the random walk; not without random walk
Status SPR at the year’s F; s for B/BtgtB/B_{tgt} under Beverton-Holt; plot_LBAdvice(flicc2FLStockR(fit))
Models gtg + dm routinely; gamma + nb to replicate fishblicc
MSE fixed sigmaF, absolute tail cut, se = FALSE; tune with the HCR

Planned: a worked example of a rebuilding stock, refitted year by year, to show how SPR, the tail cut and sigmaF respond over time; estimated Dirichlet-multinomial overdispersion.
